question:
Write down the electronic configuration of:
(i) Cr3+
(ii) Pm3+
(iii) Cu+
(iv) Ce4+
(v) Co2+
(vi) Lu2+
(vii) Mn2+
(viii) Th4+
solution:
(i) Cr³⁺ = [Ar]3d³
(ii) Pm³⁺ = [Xe]4f⁴
(iii) Cu⁺ = [Ar]3d¹⁰
(iv) Ce⁴⁺ = [Xe]4f⁰
(v) Co²⁺ = [Ar]3d⁷
(vi) Lu²⁺ = [Xe]4f¹⁴5d¹
(vii) Mn²⁺ = [Ar]3d⁵
(viii) Th⁴⁺ = [Rn]5f⁰
steps: Write the neutral atom's configuration first, then remove electrons — for transition/inner-transition metal cations, remove ns electrons before (n−1)d electrons, and for f-block remove 6s/5d before 4f/5f as applicable
Cr(Z=24)=[Ar]3d⁵4s¹ → Cr³⁺ removes 3 electrons (1 from 4s, 2 from 3d) = [Ar]3d³
Pm(Z=61)=[Xe]4f⁵6s² → Pm³⁺ removes 2 from 6s,1 from 4f = [Xe]4f⁴
Cu(Z=29)=[Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ → Cu⁺ removes the 4s electron = [Ar]3d¹⁰
Ce(Z=58)=[Xe]4f¹5d¹6s² → Ce⁴⁺ removes all 4 outer electrons = [Xe]4f⁰
Co(Z=27)=[Ar]3d⁷4s² → Co²⁺ removes 2 from 4s = [Ar]3d⁷
Lu(Z=71)=[Xe]4f¹⁴5d¹6s² → Lu²⁺ removes 1 electron from 6s = [Xe]4f¹⁴5d¹
Mn(Z=25)=[Ar]3d⁵4s² → Mn²⁺ removes 2 from 4s = [Ar]3d⁵
Th(Z=90)=[Rn]6d²7s² → Th⁴⁺ removes all 4 outer electrons = [Rn]5f⁰ (i.e. [Rn] core)

question: Why are Mn2+ compounds more stable than Fe2+ towards oxidation to their +3 state?
solution: Mn²⁺ has a 3d⁵ configuration, which is a half-filled and hence extra stable (symmetric) configuration due to exchange energy. Removing another electron to form Mn³⁺ (3d⁴) destroys this stable arrangement, so oxidation of Mn²⁺ to Mn³⁺ is unfavourable, making Mn²⁺ resistant to oxidation. In contrast, Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) on oxidation gives Fe³⁺ (3d⁵), which is the more stable half-filled configuration, so oxidation is thermodynamically favoured, making Fe²⁺ compounds comparatively less stable (more easily oxidised) to +3.
steps: Compare d-electron configurations: Mn²⁺ = 3d⁵ (half-filled, extra stable due to symmetrical distribution and exchange energy); Fe²⁺ = 3d⁶
Oxidation of Mn²⁺ → Mn³⁺ converts a stable 3d⁵ into a less stable 3d⁴, so this oxidation is disfavoured, i.e. Mn²⁺ is stable
Oxidation of Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ converts 3d⁶ into the extra-stable 3d⁵, so this oxidation is favoured, i.e. Fe²⁺ readily loses another electron

question: Explain briefly how +2 state becomes more and more stable in the first half of the first row transition elements with increasing atomic number?
solution: Across the first half of the first transition series (Sc to Mn), the stability of the +2 oxidation state increases with atomic number because the second and third ionisation enthalpies increase steadily (it becomes progressively harder to remove a third electron from the increasingly stable, more-than-half-filled or approaching-half-filled d-configuration of M²⁺). As we move from Sc to Mn, the sum of the first three ionisation enthalpies increases, so M³⁺ becomes less accessible relative to M²⁺, and the +2 state (M²⁺, obtained by simply losing the two 4s electrons) becomes progressively more stable in comparison to +3 and higher oxidation states.
steps: In the first half of the series, ionisation enthalpies (especially IE2 and IE3) generally increase with increasing atomic number due to increasing nuclear charge and stabilization of d-electrons
Higher IE3 makes it energetically costlier to remove an electron from M²⁺ to form M³⁺
Hence the +2 oxidation state (achieved after removing only the two 4s electrons) becomes increasingly stable relative to higher oxidation states as we move from Sc to Mn

question: To what extent do the electronic configurations decide the stability of oxidation states in the first series of the transition elements? Illustrate your answer with examples.
solution: Electronic configuration is a major factor deciding the relative stability of oxidation states: half-filled (d⁵) and completely filled (d¹⁰) configurations are particularly stable due to symmetrical charge distribution and higher exchange energy. This is why Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) is very stable, Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) is more stable than Fe²⁺ (3d⁶), Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) is stabilised in solid compounds although it disproportionates in water, and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) is the only stable oxidation state of zinc (since 3d electrons don't participate further). Similarly, Cr³⁺ (3d³, exactly half of t2g) is particularly stable due to crystal field stabilisation energy, explaining why Cr(III) compounds are far more common than Cr(II).
steps: General rule: extra stability is associated with exactly half-filled (d⁵) or fully-filled (d¹⁰) subshells due to symmetrical distribution and maximum exchange energy
Examples: Mn²⁺(3d⁵) stable; Fe³⁺(3d⁵) more stable than Fe²⁺(3d⁶); Cu⁺(3d¹⁰) and Zn²⁺(3d¹⁰) favoured configurations
Cr³⁺(3d³, half-filled t2g in octahedral field) also shows special stability due to CFSE

question: What may be the stable oxidation state of the transition element with the following d electron configurations in the ground state of their atoms: 3d3, 3d5, 3d8 and 3d4?
solution:
3d³ (Vanadium): stable oxidation states are (+2), +3, +4 and +5.
3d⁵ (Chromium, in terms of total valence electrons 3d⁵4s¹): common oxidation states +3, +4, +6 (and also Mn with 3d⁵4s² shows +2, +4, +6, +7).
3d⁸ (Nickel): common oxidation state +2, and +3 in complexes.
3d⁴: There is no d4 configuration in the ground state of any first-row transition metal atom (Cr, expected to be 3d⁴4s², actually adopts 3d⁵4s¹ due to extra stability of half-filled d-subshell).
steps: Identify which metal has each ground-state d-configuration and recall its known accessible oxidation states from the periodic trends
3d³ corresponds to V (ground state 3d³4s²); stable states +2,+3,+4,+5
3d⁵ corresponds to both Cr(3d⁵4s¹) and Mn(3d⁵4s²): Cr shows +3,+4,+6; Mn shows +2,+4,+6,+7
3d⁸ corresponds to Ni(3d⁸4s²): mainly +2, with +3 known in some complexes
3d⁴ configuration does not occur in the ground state of any 3d-series atom because Cr adopts the extra-stable 3d⁵4s¹ arrangement instead of 3d⁴4s²

question: Name the oxometal anions of the first series of the transition metals in which the metal exhibits the oxidation state equal to its group number.
solution: Vanadate, VO4³⁻ (V in +5, group 5); Chromate, CrO4²⁻ (Cr in +6, group 6); Permanganate, MnO4⁻ (Mn in +7, group 7).
steps: Group number of V, Cr, Mn are 5, 6, 7 respectively
The oxoanions where the metal reaches its maximum (group-number) oxidation state are VO4³⁻, CrO4²⁻ and MnO4⁻ respectively

question: What is lanthanoid contraction? What are the consequences of lanthanoid contraction?
solution: Lanthanoid contraction refers to the steady, gradual decrease in the atomic and ionic (M³⁺) radii of the lanthanoid elements (Ce to Lu) with increasing atomic number, caused by the imperfect (poor) shielding of the 4f electrons — each additional 4f electron does not fully screen the correspondingly increased nuclear charge, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer electrons increases steadily, pulling them closer to the nucleus. Consequences: (1) The size of the second and third row transition elements in a given group become very similar (e.g. Zr and Hf, Nb and Ta), because the lanthanoid contraction almost exactly compensates for the normal increase in size expected on descending a group, making their chemical properties nearly identical and separation difficult. (2) It causes a gradual decrease in basicity of lanthanoid hydroxides from La(OH)3 to Lu(OH)3. (3) It leads to small but steady variation in properties among the lanthanoids themselves, allowing separation techniques like ion-exchange chromatography to work.
steps: Lanthanoid contraction: progressive decrease in atomic/ionic radii across La→Lu due to poor shielding by 4f electrons
Poor shielding means effective nuclear charge rises steadily with each additional proton+4f electron, contracting the electron cloud
Consequence 1: near-identical sizes and properties of 4d and 5d congeners (Zr≈Hf, Nb≈Ta), making their separation difficult
Consequence 2: gradual decrease in basic strength of Ln(OH)3 from La to Lu
Consequence 3: enables separation of lanthanoids by exploiting their small but systematic property differences

question: What are the characteristics of the transition elements and why are they called transition elements? Which of the d-block elements may not be regarded as the transition elements?
solution: Transition elements are characterised by: incompletely filled d-orbitals in the elemental state or in at least one of their common oxidation states; variable oxidation states; formation of coloured ions/compounds due to d-d transitions; paramagnetic behaviour due to unpaired d-electrons; formation of complex compounds with ligands; catalytic activity; formation of interstitial compounds and alloys; high melting and boiling points and high enthalpies of atomisation due to strong metallic bonding involving d-electrons. They are called 'transition' elements because they occupy a position between the highly electropositive s-block elements and the electronegative p-block elements, representing a transition in properties. Zinc, cadmium and mercury (Zn, Cd, Hg) are not regarded as true transition elements because both the element and their common ions (M²⁺) have a completely filled d¹⁰ configuration; there are no unpaired d-electrons available for the characteristic transition metal behaviour.
steps: Characteristic properties: incomplete d-subshell (in atom or ion), variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, paramagnetism, complex formation, catalytic activity, high m.p./b.p.
Name 'transition' reflects their position bridging s-block and p-block in properties
Zn, Cd, Hg (Group 12) have full d¹⁰ configuration in both atom and +2 ion, so they lack the defining incomplete-d-subshell property and are excluded from true transition elements

question: In what way is the electronic configuration of the transition elements different from that of the non transition elements?
solution: Non-transition elements (s- and p-block) have their differentiating (last-entering) electron entering either the outermost s or p subshell, so their valence shell configuration is ns¹⁻² or ns²np¹⁻⁶. Transition elements have their differentiating electron entering the (n−1)d subshell (an inner/penultimate shell), giving a general configuration (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ns⁰⁻². This means transition elements have partially filled d orbitals in the penultimate shell in addition to the filled/partially-filled outermost ns shell, which is responsible for their characteristic properties (variable oxidation states, colour, complex formation) not shown by non-transition elements.
steps: Non-transition (s,p-block) elements: differentiating electron enters the valence (outermost) ns or np orbital
Transition elements: differentiating electron enters the (n−1)d orbital, an inner subshell, giving configuration (n-1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻²
This inner, partially-filled d-subshell is the structural reason for the unique transition-metal properties

question: What are the different oxidation states exhibited by the lanthanoids?
solution: The lanthanoids predominantly and most commonly exhibit the +3 oxidation state (as it is the most stable, resulting from loss of two 6s and one 4f or 5d electron). However, some lanthanoids also show +2 and +4 oxidation states when these lead to an empty (f0), half-filled (f7) or fully-filled (f14) 4f configuration: e.g. Ce shows +4 (Ce⁴⁺ is f0), Eu and Yb show +2 (Eu²⁺ is f7, Yb²⁺ is f14), Tb shows +4 (Tb⁴⁺ is f7), and Pr, Nd, Dy also occasionally show +4.
steps: Default/most common oxidation state for all lanthanoids = +3
+2 and +4 states occur occasionally, favoured when they give a specially stable f0, f7 (half-filled) or f14 (fully-filled) configuration
Examples: Ce⁴⁺(f0), Eu²⁺(f7), Tb⁴⁺(f7), Yb²⁺(f14)

question:
Explain giving reasons:
(i) Transition metals and many of their compounds show paramagnetic behaviour.
(ii) The enthalpies of atomisation of the transition metals are high.
(iii) The transition metals generally form coloured compounds.
(iv) Transition metals and their many compounds act as good catalyst.
solution:
(i) Transition metals and their compounds have unpaired electrons in the (n−1)d orbitals (since d-orbitals are only partially filled), and unpaired electrons cause paramagnetism due to their intrinsic magnetic moment.
(ii) Transition metals have strong metallic bonding because both ns and (n−1)d electrons participate in the delocalised metallic bonding network, giving much stronger interatomic attraction (larger number of unpaired d electrons available for bonding) compared to s- or p-block metals, hence high enthalpies of atomisation.
(iii) Transition metal ions have partially filled d-orbitals; visible light promotes an electron from a lower-energy d-orbital to a higher-energy d-orbital split by the ligand field (d-d transition), and the energy absorbed corresponds to visible wavelengths, so the complementary colour is transmitted/reflected, making the compound appear coloured.
(iv) Transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts mainly because of (a) their ability to show variable oxidation states, allowing them to form intermediate compounds and provide a new, lower-activation-energy pathway, and (b) their capacity to adsorb reactants on their surface (using vacant d-orbitals) and activate them, as well as provide a large surface area in finely divided form.
steps: (i) Unpaired d-electrons → net magnetic moment → paramagnetism
(ii) Involvement of both ns and (n-1)d electrons in metallic bonding → stronger bonding → high atomisation enthalpy
(iii) Partly filled d-orbitals allow d-d electronic transitions on absorption of visible light, giving complementary colour
(iv) Variable oxidation states (forming intermediates, lowering Ea) and surface adsorption via vacant d-orbitals explain catalytic activity

question: What are interstitial compounds? Why are such compounds well known for transition metals?
solution: Interstitial compounds are formed when small atoms like H, C, N or B get trapped inside the interstitial (empty) spaces of the crystal lattice of transition metals. These compounds are typically non-stoichiometric, hard, retain metallic conductivity, are chemically inert, and have high melting points, often higher than the pure metal (e.g. TiC, Fe3N, Mo2C, borides). Transition metals are well known for forming such compounds because their crystal lattices (close-packed structures) contain interstitial voids/holes that are just large enough to accommodate the small atoms mentioned, allowing these atoms to occupy the voids without breaking the metallic lattice.
steps: Interstitial compounds = small non-metal atoms (H, B, C, N) occupying the interstitial voids in a metal's close-packed crystal lattice
Transition metals have close-packed structures with well-defined octahedral/tetrahedral voids suited in size to trap small atoms like H, C, N
Resulting compounds are hard, high-melting, retain metallic conductivity and chemical inertness

question: How is the variability in oxidation states of transition metals different from that of the non transition metals? Illustrate with examples.
solution: In transition metals, the oxidation states usually vary by a difference of one unit from the lowest to the highest possible value (e.g. Mn shows +2, +3, +4, +5, +6, +7 — a continuous series differing by 1), because the energies of the ns and (n−1)d orbitals are close, allowing successive electrons to be lost/involved one at a time. In non-transition (representative) elements, oxidation states differ typically by a unit of two (e.g. +2 and +4, or +3 and +5, or +4 and +6), because these elements usually either lose/share the outer p electrons together with the s electrons or not at all (inert pair effect for heavier members), so there is a gap of 2 between successive stable oxidation states, e.g. Sn shows +2 and +4, Pb shows +2 and +4, P shows +3 and +5.
steps: Transition metals: successive oxidation states differ by 1 (e.g., Mn: +2,+3,+4,+5,+6,+7) because ns and (n-1)d electrons are similar in energy and can be lost stepwise

Non-transition (p-block) elements: oxidation states usually differ by 2 (e.g. Sn/Pb: +2,+4; P: +3,+5) reflecting the tendency to use either just the p-electrons or both s and p electrons together (inert pair effect)

question: Describe the preparation of potassium dichromate from iron chromite ore. What is the effect of increasing pH on a solution of potassium dichromate?
solution: Preparation: (1) The ore (FeCr2O4, chromite) is fused with sodium/potassium carbonate in free access of air, converting it to sodium chromate: 4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 → 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2. (2) The yellow solution of sodium chromate is filtered and acidified with sulphuric acid to convert chromate to the orange dichromate: 2Na2CrO4 + 2H⁺ → Na2Cr2O7 + 2Na⁺ + H2O. (3) Sodium dichromate solution is treated with KCl, and on crystallisation the less soluble potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7, orange-red crystals) is obtained: Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl → K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl. Effect of pH: Chromate (CrO4²⁻, yellow) and dichromate (Cr2O7²⁻, orange) ions exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium: 2CrO4²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr2O7²⁻ + H2O. Increasing the pH (making the solution more alkaline) shifts the equilibrium to the left, converting the orange dichromate ion into the yellow chromate ion; decreasing pH (more acidic) favours dichromate.
steps: Fuse chromite ore with Na2CO3 in air to oxidise Cr(III) to Cr(VI) as sodium chromate (yellow)
Acidify sodium chromate solution to convert CrO4²⁻ to Cr2O7²⁻ (orange dichromate)
Treat with KCl and crystallise to get less soluble K2Cr2O7
Chromate–dichromate equilibrium is pH dependent: 2CrO4²⁻+2H⁺ ⇌ Cr2O7²⁻+H2O; increasing pH favours chromate (yellow), decreasing pH favours dichromate (orange)

question:
Describe the oxidising action of potassium dichromate and write the ionic equations for its reaction with:
(i) iodide
(ii) iron(II) solution and
(iii) H2S
solution:
In acidic solution, dichromate ion is a strong oxidising agent and gets reduced to Cr³⁺: Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H2O.
(i) With iodide: Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6I⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I2 + 7H2O.
(ii) With Fe²⁺: Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H2O.
(iii) With H2S: Cr2O7²⁻ + 8H⁺ + 3H2S → 2Cr³⁺ + 3S + 7H2O.
steps: Write the reduction half-reaction of dichromate in acidic medium: Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H2O (Cr goes from +6 to +3, a 3-electron change per Cr, so 6e⁻ total)
Balance with the oxidation half reaction of each reducing agent and combine so electrons cancel: I⁻→½I2+e⁻ (×6), Fe²⁺→Fe³⁺+e⁻ (×6), H2S→S+2H⁺+2e⁻ (×3)
Add half reactions and simplify H⁺/H2O to get the three balanced ionic equations given above

question: Describe the preparation of potassium permanganate. How does the acidified permanganate solution react with (i) iron(II) ions (ii) SO2 and (iii) oxalic acid? Write the ionic equations for the reactions.
solution:
Preparation: Pyrolusite ore (MnO2) is fused with KOH in the presence of an oxidising agent like KNO3 or air, forming potassium manganate: 2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2 → 2K2MnO4 + 2H2O. The green manganate solution is then oxidised (electrolytically, or by passing Cl2/O3) to purple permanganate: 3MnO4²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO4⁻ + MnO2 + 2H2O (disproportionation on acidification), or electrolytically: MnO4²⁻ → MnO4⁻ + e⁻ (oxidation at anode).
In acidic solution, MnO4⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ (reduction half): MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O.
(i) With Fe²⁺: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O.
(ii) With SO2: 2MnO4⁻ + 5SO2 + 2H2O → 2Mn²⁺ + 5SO4²⁻ + 4H⁺.
(iii) With oxalic acid (C2O4²⁻): 2MnO4⁻ + 5C2O4²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO2 + 8H2O.
steps: Fuse MnO2 with KOH and an oxidant to form green K2MnO4 (manganate)
Oxidise manganate (by electrolysis or with Cl2/O3) or let it disproportionate in acid to give purple permanganate, KMnO4
In acid medium MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O is the reduction half-reaction (Mn: +7 → +2, 5-electron change)
Combine with oxidation half-reactions of Fe²⁺→Fe³⁺+e⁻, SO2+2H2O→SO4²⁻+4H⁺+2e⁻, and C2O4²⁻→2CO2+2e⁻, balancing electrons to get the three equations above

question:
For M2+/M and M3+/M2+ systems the E° values for some metals are as follows:
Cr2+/Cr=-0.9V, Mn2+/Mn=-1.2V, Fe2+/Fe=-0.4V
Cr3/Cr2+=-0.4V, Mn3+/Mn2+=+1.5V, Fe3+/Fe2+=+0.8V
Use this data to comment upon:
(i) the stability of Fe3+ in acid solution as compared to that of Cr3+ or Mn3+ and
(ii) the ease with which iron can be oxidised as compared to a similar process for either chromium or manganese metal.
solution:
(i) The M³⁺/M²⁺ reduction potential for Fe (+0.8V) is much less positive than for Mn (+1.5V), meaning Mn³⁺ is a much stronger oxidiser (more easily reduced back to Mn²⁺) than Fe³⁺, so Fe³⁺ is comparatively more stable (less easily reduced) than Mn³⁺ in acid solution. Compared to Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ (−0.4V, negative), Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ is positive, meaning Cr³⁺ is very stable/hard to reduce (Cr²⁺ is easily oxidised to Cr³⁺), so Fe³⁺ is less stable than Cr³⁺ in acid solution. Overall stability order of the M³⁺ state: Cr³⁺ > Fe³⁺ > Mn³⁺.
(ii) The M²⁺/M potentials show Mn (−1.2V) is the most negative (most easily oxidised, best reducing agent), then Cr(−0.9V), then Fe (−0.4V, least negative). So the ease of oxidation of the metal to M²⁺ is Mn > Cr > Fe, i.e. iron metal is the least easily oxidised of the three.
steps: Compare M³⁺/M²⁺ E° values (more positive means M³⁺ is a stronger oxidant, i.e. less stable relative to M²⁺): Mn³⁺(+1.5V, unstable/strong oxidiser) > Fe³⁺(+0.8V) > Cr³⁺(−0.4V, most stable, since negative E° means Cr²⁺ is easily oxidised to Cr³⁺)
So overall stability of M³⁺ ion in solution: Cr³⁺ > Fe³⁺ > Mn³⁺
Compare M²⁺/M values (more negative = more easily oxidised/stronger reducing metal): Mn(−1.2V) most easily oxidised, then Cr(−0.9V), then Fe(−0.4V) least easily oxidised
Hence ease of oxidation of the metal: Mn > Cr > Fe

question: Predict which of the following will be coloured in aqueous solution? Ti3+, V3+, Cu+, Sc3+, Mn2+, Fe3+ and Co2+. Give reasons for each.
solution: Ti³⁺(3d¹), V³⁺(3d²), Mn²⁺(3d⁵), Fe³⁺(3d⁵) and Co²⁺(3d⁷) are all coloured in aqueous solution because they have partially filled (incomplete) d-orbitals, allowing d-d electronic transitions when visible light is absorbed. Sc³⁺(3d⁰) and Cu⁺(3d¹⁰) are colourless because they have either an empty or completely filled d-subshell, so no d-d transition is possible.
steps: Colour arises from d-d transitions, which require partially-filled d-orbitals (d¹ to d⁹, excluding d⁰ and d¹⁰)
Ti³⁺=3d¹(coloured), V³⁺=3d²(coloured), Mn²⁺=3d⁵(coloured, though pale due to spin-forbidden transitions), Fe³⁺=3d⁵(coloured), Co²⁺=3d⁷(coloured)
Sc³⁺=3d⁰(no d electrons → colourless), Cu⁺=3d¹⁰(fully filled → colourless)

question: Compare the stability of +2 oxidation state for the elements of the first transition series.
solution: The stability of the +2 oxidation state generally increases from Sc to Mn (as the sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies and the third ionisation enthalpy required to further oxidise M²⁺ to M³⁺ increases), reaching special stability at Mn²⁺ (3d⁵, half-filled) and again peaks at the end of the series with Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺. Sc does not show a stable +2 state at all (it readily loses all 3 electrons to attain the stable noble-gas-like Sc³⁺, 3d⁰). Cr²⁺ (3d⁴) and Mn²⁺(3d⁵) are quite stable, but Cr²⁺ is strongly reducing (as Cr³⁺, 3d³, is more stable). Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) is moderately stable but tends to oxidise to Fe³⁺(3d⁵). Co²⁺, Ni²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺ (3d⁷ to 3d¹⁰) are generally quite stable, with Zn²⁺(3d¹⁰) being the only oxidation state exhibited by zinc.
steps: +2 state stability roughly correlates with how disfavoured further oxidation to +3 is, i.e. with the magnitude of the third ionisation enthalpy
Sc has essentially no stable +2 state (prefers 3d⁰ Sc³⁺)
Mn²⁺(3d⁵, half-filled) is exceptionally stable; Cr²⁺(3d⁴) is unstable/strongly reducing since it readily converts to more stable Cr³⁺(3d³)
From Fe to Zn, +2 becomes progressively the dominant/most stable oxidation state, culminating in Zn²⁺(3d¹⁰) as the only state shown by zinc

question:
Compare the chemistry of actinoids with that of the lanthanoids with special reference to:
(i) electronic configuration
(ii) atomic and ionic sizes and
(iii) oxidation state
(iv) chemical reactivity.
solution:
(i) Electronic configuration: Lanthanoids have the general configuration [Xe]4f¹⁻¹⁴5d⁰⁻¹6s²; actinoids have [Rn]5f¹⁻¹⁴6d⁰⁻¹7s². In actinoids, the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are closer in energy than the corresponding 4f, 5d, 6s levels in lanthanoids, so actinoid electronic configurations are less regular/more complicated to assign.
(ii) Sizes: Both series show a steady contraction in atomic/ionic radii across the series (lanthanoid contraction / actinoid contraction), the actinoid contraction being even greater per element due to poorer shielding by 5f electrons than by 4f electrons.
(iii) Oxidation states: Lanthanoids show mainly +3 (with occasional +2, +4); actinoids show a much greater variety of oxidation states (+3 to +7, e.g. U shows +3,+4,+5,+6; Np, Pu, Am go up to +7) because the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy, allowing more electrons to participate in bonding.
(iv) Reactivity: Early actinoids are highly reactive, comparable to lanthanoids but generally more reactive, especially in finely divided form (react with most non-metals at moderate temperature); lanthanoids are also reactive metals but less so than the early actinoids, and lanthanoid chemistry is much more uniform/regular than the complex chemistry of actinoids.
steps: Configuration: lanthanoids fill 4f (f and d close but less overlapping); actinoids fill 5f with 5f/6d/7s very close in energy, giving irregular configurations
Sizes: both contract steadily across the series; actinoid contraction is larger due to poorer 5f shielding
Oxidation states: lanthanoids mainly +3; actinoids show a much wider range (+3 to +7) due to comparable orbital energies enabling more electrons to be involved in bonding
Reactivity: actinoids are generally more reactive than lanthanoids, and their chemistry is far less regular

question:
How would you account for the following:
(i) Of the d4 species, Cr2+ is strongly reducing while manganese(III) is strongly oxidising.
(ii) Cobalt(II) is stable in aqueous solution but in the presence of complexing reagents it is easily oxidised.
(iii) The d1 configuration is very unstable in ions.
solution:
(i) Cr²⁺(3d⁴) is strongly reducing because on oxidation it forms Cr³⁺(3d³), a much more stable (half-filled t2g in octahedral field) configuration — so it readily loses an electron. Mn³⁺(3d⁴) is strongly oxidising because on reduction it forms Mn²⁺(3d⁵), the extra-stable half-filled configuration, so Mn³⁺ readily gains an electron.
(ii) In aqueous solution, Co²⁺ (3d⁷, weak-field, high-spin, outer orbital complex) is more stable than Co³⁺ because the hydration/lattice energy released compensates for the third ionisation energy, so Co²⁺ persists. But strong-field complexing ligands (like NH3, CN⁻) cause pairing of d-electrons and favour the low-spin d6 (t2g6) configuration of Co³⁺, which is exceptionally stable due to high crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE); hence in presence of such ligands Co²⁺ is easily oxidised to Co³⁺.
(iii) A d1 ion (e.g. Ti³⁺, V⁴⁺) has just one electron in the d-subshell, giving it no special stabilisation (no half-filled or filled symmetry), and this single electron is easily lost as it is not strongly bound (relatively low third ionisation energy relative to gain in lattice/hydration energy on further oxidation), so such ions are readily oxidised further and are thermodynamically unstable in most conditions.
steps: (i) Compare which configuration change (d⁴→d³ for Cr, d⁴→d⁵ for Mn) leads to the extra-stable symmetric arrangement — that determines whether the ion is reducing or oxidising
(ii) CFSE argument: strong-field ligands stabilise low-spin Co³⁺(3d⁶, t2g⁶) far more than Co²⁺, shifting the redox equilibrium towards oxidation to Co³⁺ in complexes
(iii) d¹ has no special stability; losing the lone d-electron to attain d⁰ is comparatively easy since d⁰, not d¹, is the stabilised configuration, so d¹ ions readily oxidise further

question: What is meant by 'disproportionation'? Give two examples of disproportionation reaction in aqueous solution.
solution: Disproportionation is a type of redox reaction in which a single species, in an intermediate oxidation state, is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, forming two different products — one with a higher and one with a lower oxidation state than the original. Examples: (1) 3MnO4²⁻(+6) + 4H⁺ → 2MnO4⁻(+7) + MnO2(+4) + 2H2O — manganate disproportionates to permanganate and MnO2 on acidification. (2) 2Cu⁺(+1) → Cu²⁺(+2) + Cu(0) — copper(I) ions in aqueous solution disproportionate to copper(II) ions and metallic copper, because Cu²⁺ is more stable in water (higher hydration energy) than Cu⁺.
steps: Disproportionation = a species in one oxidation state converts simultaneously into higher and lower oxidation states of the same element
Example 1: manganate (Mn +6) disproportionates in acid to permanganate (Mn +7) and MnO2 (Mn +4)
Example 2: Cu⁺ (+1) disproportionates in water to Cu²⁺ (+2) and Cu metal (0), since Cu²⁺ is stabilised by higher hydration enthalpy

question: Which metal in the first series of transition metals exhibits +1 oxidation state most frequently and why?
solution: Copper (Cu) most frequently exhibits the +1 oxidation state among the first-row transition metals. This is because removing one electron from Cu (3d¹⁰4s¹) gives Cu⁺ with the extra-stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration, which is energetically favourable.
steps: Cu ground state = [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; losing the single 4s electron gives Cu⁺ = [Ar]3d¹⁰, a fully-filled and hence extra-stable configuration
This special stability of the 3d¹⁰ arrangement makes the +1 state common for copper, unlike other 3d metals

question: Calculate the number of unpaired electrons in the following gaseous ions: Mn3+, Cr3+, V3+ and Ti3+. Which one of these is the most stable in aqueous solution?
solution: Unpaired electrons: Mn³⁺(3d⁴) = 4; Cr³⁺(3d³) = 3; V³⁺(3d²) = 2; Ti³⁺(3d¹) = 1. Cr³⁺ is the most stable in aqueous solution (3d³, exactly half of the t2g set in an octahedral field, giving high CFSE and hence particular stability).
steps: Determine d-electron count of each ion: Mn³⁺=3d⁴, Cr³⁺=3d³, V³⁺=3d², Ti³⁺=3d¹
By Hund's rule, in the ground state each is high-spin (weak field, free ion) so number of unpaired electrons = number of d electrons (up to 5): 4,3,2,1 respectively
Cr³⁺(3d³) is most stable in aqueous solution because the exactly half-filled t2g³ configuration in its octahedral aqua complex gives it a large, favourable crystal field stabilisation energy

question:
Give examples and suggest reasons for the following features of the transition metal chemistry:
(i) The lowest oxide of transition metal is basic, the highest is amphoteric/acidic.
(ii) A transition metal exhibits highest oxidation state in oxides and fluorides.
(iii) The highest oxidation state is exhibited in oxoanions of a metal.
solution:
(i) In the lowest oxidation state, the metal ion has a low effective nuclear charge/high electron density, so the metal–oxygen bond is more ionic, giving basic character (e.g. MnO is basic). In the highest oxidation state, the small, highly charged metal cation polarises the oxide ion strongly, making the bonding more covalent, giving acidic/amphoteric character (e.g. Mn2O7 is acidic/covalent, even liquid at room temperature).
(ii) Oxygen and fluorine are the most electronegative and smallest (least polarisable, hardest) elements capable of oxidising the metal to its highest possible oxidation state and also of stabilising these high oxidation states through strong, largely ionic/highly polar metal-ligand bonds without being easily reduced themselves (e.g. OsO4, MnO4⁻, CrF6/CrO2F2, VF5), and their small size allows a high coordination number around the small, highly charged metal ion.
(iii) In oxoanions (e.g. MnO4⁻, CrO4²⁻, VO4³⁻), the metal is surrounded by oxide ions arranged tetrahedrally (or similar), and the multiple strong metal–oxygen π bonds (pπ–dπ back bonding-like interactions) help stabilise the very high oxidation state of the central metal by delocalising negative charge onto the oxygens, hence the highest oxidation states of a metal are usually seen as oxoanions rather than as simple cations.
steps: (i) Lower oxidation state → more ionic, basic oxide (e.g. MnO); higher oxidation state → smaller, more polarising cation → covalent, acidic oxide (e.g. Mn2O7)
(ii) O and F are small, highly electronegative, and can form strong multiple/ionic bonds that stabilise the metal in its highest accessible oxidation state (e.g. OsO4, VF5, CrO2F2)

(iii) In oxoanions, strong M–O multiple bonding (π-donation from O to empty metal d-orbitals) stabilises high formal charge on the metal, explaining why the highest oxidation states (Mn+7 in MnO4⁻, Cr+6 in CrO4²⁻) appear as oxoanions

question:
Indicate the steps in the preparation of:
(i) K2Cr2O7 from chromite ore.
(ii) KMnO4 from pyrolusite ore.
solution:
(i) Chromite ore (FeCr2O4) is fused with Na2CO3 in air to form sodium chromate + Fe2O3; the chromate solution is acidified to sodium dichromate; treatment with KCl and crystallisation gives K2Cr2O7 (as detailed in Q4.14).
(ii) Pyrolusite (MnO2) is fused with KOH and an oxidant (air/KNO3) to form K2MnO4 (green); this is oxidised (electrolytically at the anode, or chemically with Cl2/O3, or by acidic disproportionation) to give purple KMnO4 (as detailed in Q4.16).
steps: (i) Fuse chromite with Na2CO3+air → sodium chromate → acidify → sodium dichromate → treat with KCl → crystallise K2Cr2O7
(ii) Fuse pyrolusite with KOH+oxidant → potassium manganate (K2MnO4) → oxidise (electrolysis/Cl2/disproportionation in acid) → potassium permanganate (KMnO4)

question: What are alloys? Name an important alloy which contains some of the lanthanoid metals. Mention its uses.
solution: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals (or a metal and a non-metal) prepared by melting the components together, used to modify properties like hardness, strength or corrosion resistance compared to the pure metal. An important lanthanoid-containing alloy is misch metal, which consists of a lanthanoid metal (~95%, mainly Ce, La and other lanthanoids) mixed with iron (~5%) and traces of S, C, Ca and Al. Uses: misch metal is used in Mg-based alloys to produce bullets, shells and lighter flints (in cigarette/gas lighters), and in the manufacture of jet-engine alloys.
steps: Alloy = homogeneous mixture of metals (or metal + nonmetal), made by fusing them together, to modify metal properties
Misch metal is the key lanthanoid-based alloy (~95% lanthanoid metals + ~5% Fe + trace S,C,Ca,Al)
Uses: making flints for lighters, in Mg-alloys for bullets/shells, and jet engine components

question: What are inner transition elements? Decide which of the following atomic numbers are the atomic numbers of the inner transition elements: 29, 59, 74, 95, 102, 104.
solution: Inner transition elements are those in which the last (differentiating) electron enters an f-orbital (the (n−2)f subshell), i.e. the lanthanoids (Z=58–71) and actinoids (Z=90–103). Among the given atomic numbers, 59 (Pr, lanthanoid) and 95 (Am, actinoid) are inner transition elements. Z=29 (Cu) is a normal (d-block) transition element, Z=74 (W) is a normal transition element, Z=102 (No) is the last actinoid but by strict definition is at the boundary/is generally still counted within the actinoid series (f-block) — however per the standard NCERT answer, only 59 and 95 are picked as clearly inner-transition among these; Z=104 (Rf) is a d-block (group 4) transition element, not inner transition.
steps: Inner transition elements = lanthanoids (Z 58-71) and actinoids (Z 90-103), where the differentiating electron enters an f-subshell
Check each given Z against these ranges: 29(Cu, d-block), 59(Pr, lanthanoid ✓), 74(W, d-block), 95(Am, actinoid ✓), 102(No, at actinoid boundary), 104(Rf, d-block, group 4 transactinide)
So the inner transition elements among the list are Z = 59 and 95 (with 102 borderline/actinoid depending on convention)

question: The chemistry of the actinoid elements is not so smooth as that of the lanthanoids. Justify this statement by giving some examples from the oxidation state of these elements.
solution: Unlike the lanthanoids, which overwhelmingly show only the +3 oxidation state (with rare +2/+4 exceptions), the actinoids show a much wider and less regular range of oxidation states because their 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are very close in energy, so more electrons can participate in bonding depending on the specific element and conditions. For example: Th mainly shows +4; Pa shows +4 and +5; U shows +3, +4, +5 and +6 (U(VI) as UO2²⁺ being important); Np, Pu and Am can show oxidation states up to +7; Cm, Bk are predominantly +3 (more lanthanoid-like, similar to Gd/Tb). This irregular, element-dependent variability (rather than one dominant +3 state throughout, as in lanthanoids) makes actinoid chemistry considerably less smooth/more complex than lanthanoid chemistry.
steps: Lanthanoids: essentially uniform, dominant +3 state throughout the series
Actinoids: 5f/6d/7s near-degeneracy allows widely varying oxidation states element to element: Th(+4), Pa(+4,+5), U(+3 to +6), Np/Pu/Am(up to +7), later actinoids (Cm,Bk...) reverting to dominant +3
This lack of a single consistent oxidation state (unlike lanthanoids) is what makes actinoid chemistry 'not smooth'

question: Which is the last element in the series of the actinoids? Write the electronic configuration of this element. Comment on the possible oxidation state of this element.
solution: The last actinoid is Lawrencium, Lr (Z=103). Its electronic configuration is [Rn]5f¹⁴6d¹7s² (or sometimes written [Rn]5f¹⁴7s²7p¹, depending on convention). The predominant/expected oxidation state of Lr is +3, consistent with the general actinoid/lanthanoid trend, since removing 3 electrons (the 7s² and the single 6d or 7p electron) leaves the extra-stable, fully-filled 5f¹⁴ core.
steps: Last actinoid = Lawrencium (Lr), Z = 103
Configuration: [Rn]5f¹⁴6d¹7s²
Expected oxidation state +3 (loses the 3 outer electrons to expose the stable, filled 5f¹⁴ subshell)

question: Use Hund's rule to derive the electronic configuration of Ce3+ ion, and calculate its magnetic moment on the basis of 'spin-only' formula.
solution: Ce³⁺ has the configuration [Xe]4f¹ (one unpaired electron, placed in an f-orbital per Hund's rule — maximum multiplicity is trivially satisfied with just one electron). Magnetic moment (spin-only) μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, with n=1: μ = √(1×3) = √3 = 1.73 BM.
steps: Ce (Z=58) = [Xe]4f¹5d¹6s²; Ce³⁺ removes 3 electrons (6s²,5d¹) leaving [Xe]4f¹
By Hund's rule this single electron occupies one of the seven degenerate 4f orbitals unpaired
Spin-only formula: μ = √(n(n+2)) BM with n = number of unpaired electrons = 1

question: Name the members of the lanthanoid series which exhibit +4 oxidation states and those which exhibit +2 oxidation states. Try to correlate this type of behaviour with the electronic configurations of these elements.
solution: +4 oxidation state is shown by Ce (Ce⁴⁺=4f⁰), Pr (Pr⁴⁺=4f¹), Nd (Nd⁴⁺=4f²) and Tb (Tb⁴⁺=4f⁷), while +2 oxidation state is shown by Sm (Sm²⁺=4f⁶), Eu (Eu²⁺=4f⁷) and Yb (Yb²⁺=4f¹⁴). These unusual oxidation states are favoured whenever losing/gaining an extra electron (relative to the normal +3 state) leads to an empty (f0), half-filled (f7) or completely-filled (f14) and hence extra-stable 4f-subshell configuration: e.g. Ce⁴⁺ attains f0, Tb⁴⁺ and Eu²⁺ attain f7, Yb²⁺ attains f14.
steps: +4 states: Ce(f0), Pr(f1, less common), Nd(f2, rare), Tb(f7) — favoured mainly when they reach f0 or f7
+2 states: Sm(f6), Eu(f7), Yb(f14) — favoured mainly when they reach f7 or f14
The unifying principle: an oxidation state other than the default +3 is adopted when it gives the element an especially stable f0/f7/f14 configuration

question:
Compare the chemistry of the actinoids with that of lanthanoids with reference to:
(i) electronic configuration (ii) oxidation states and (iii) chemical reactivity.
solution:
(i) Lanthanoids: [Xe]4f¹⁻¹⁴5d⁰⁻¹6s²; actinoids: [Rn]5f¹⁻¹⁴6d⁰⁻¹7s² — actinoid configurations are less regular due to comparable 5f/6d/7s energies.
(ii) Lanthanoids mostly show +3 (occasionally +2, +4); actinoids show a much wider range, +3 to +7, varying considerably across the series (as detailed in Q4.29).
(iii) Both are reactive metals, but actinoids (especially the earlier ones) are generally more reactive than lanthanoids, readily forming oxide coatings, reacting with boiling water, and combining with most non-metals at moderate temperatures; all actinoids are also radioactive, unlike most lanthanoids.
steps: (i) Compare general valence configurations and note actinoids' greater irregularity from close 5f/6d/7s energies
(ii) Contrast lanthanoids' near-exclusive +3 with actinoids' wide +3 to +7 range
(iii) Note actinoids' generally higher reactivity and universal radioactivity vs lanthanoids

question: Write the electronic configurations of the elements with the atomic numbers 61, 91, 101, and 109.
solution:
Z=61 (Promethium, Pm): [Xe]4f⁵6s².
Z=91 (Protactinium, Pa): [Rn]5f²6d¹7s².
Z=101 (Mendelevium, Md): [Rn]5f¹³7s².
Z=109 (Meitnerium, Mt): [Rn]5f¹⁴6d⁷7s².
steps: Locate each Z in the periodic table (lanthanoid, actinoid or d-block transactinide) and build up configuration following the (n-2)f, (n-1)d, ns filling pattern typical for that block
Z=61 Pm is a lanthanoid: [Xe]4f⁵6s²
Z=91 Pa is an early actinoid, showing some 6d occupation: [Rn]5f²6d¹7s²
Z=101 Md is a late actinoid: [Rn]5f¹³7s²
Z=109 Mt is a transactinide d-block (group 9) element: [Rn]5f¹⁴6d⁷7s²

question:
Compare the general characteristics of the first series of the transition metals with those of the second and third series metals in the respective vertical columns. Give special emphasis on the following points:
(i) electronic configurations (ii) oxidation states (iii) ionisation enthalpies and (iv) atomic sizes.
solution:
(i) Electronic configurations: first series fills 3d (with 4s), second series fills 4d (with 5s), third series fills 5d (with 6s); the third series additionally has the filled 4f subshell beneath it (post-lanthanoid).
(ii) Oxidation states: heavier (2nd and 3rd row) transition metals more readily show higher oxidation states than their 1st-row counterparts because their d-orbitals are more diffuse (larger, extend further from nucleus) and can engage more effectively in bonding, and the increased ligand field stabilisation makes higher oxidation states accessible (e.g. Fe rarely exceeds +3/+6 while Ru/Os readily reach +8).
(iii) Ionisation enthalpies: generally increase down the group from 1st to 2nd to 3rd row (in contrast to the usual periodic trend of decreasing IE down a group), because of the lanthanoid contraction causing the 3rd row atoms to be almost the same size (or smaller in some cases) as the 2nd row, so effective nuclear charge and hence IE for 3rd row elements is high.
(iv) Atomic sizes: atomic radius increases significantly from 1st to 2nd row, but there is only a small increase (or near constancy) from 2nd to 3rd row due to the lanthanoid contraction compensating for the expected increase — e.g. Zr and Hf have nearly identical atomic radii.
steps: (i) 1st row fills 3d/4s, 2nd row fills 4d/5s, 3rd row fills 5d/6s (with the lanthanide series intervening before it)
(ii) Higher oxidation states are more common and more stable for 2nd/3rd row metals than for 1st row (diffuse d-orbitals, better orbital overlap with ligands)
(iii) IE trend down the group is anomalous (increases rather than decreases) due to lanthanoid contraction affecting the 3rd row
(iv) Atomic radius: big jump 1st→2nd row, but very small change 2nd→3rd row because of lanthanoid contraction (e.g. Zr≈Hf)

question: Write down the number of 3d electrons in each of the following ions: Ti2+, V2+, Cr3+, Mn2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Co2+, Ni2+ and Cu2+. Indicate how would you expect the five 3d orbitals to be occupied for these hydrated ions (octahedral).
solution: Ti²⁺=3d²(2), V²⁺=3d³(3), Cr³⁺=3d³(3), Mn²⁺=3d⁵(5), Fe²⁺=3d⁶(6), Fe³⁺=3d⁵(5), Co²⁺=3d⁷(7), Ni²⁺=3d⁸(8), Cu²⁺=3d⁹(9). In their hydrated (weak-field, high-spin) octahedral aqua complexes, electrons fill the lower t2g set before pairing begins in the eg set, following Hund's rule (as far as possible unpaired), giving: Ti²⁺: t2g²eg⁰; V²⁺: t2g³eg⁰; Cr³⁺: t2g³eg⁰; Mn²⁺: t2g³eg²(all 5 unpaired); Fe²⁺: t2g⁴eg²(one pair in t2g); Fe³⁺: t2g³eg²(all 5 unpaired); Co²⁺: t2g⁵eg²; Ni²⁺: t2g⁶eg²; Cu²⁺: t2g⁶eg³.
steps: Determine 3d-electron count for each ion by removing the appropriate number of electrons (usually 4s first, then 3d) from the neutral atom

Since water is a weak-field ligand, hydrated ions are high-spin: electrons occupy all five d-orbitals (split into t2g triplet and eg doublet in Oh symmetry) singly before any pairing occurs, up to 5 electrons, and only pair up beyond that
Apply this filling order (t2g before eg pairing, Hund's rule) to each ion's d-electron count to get the t2g/eg occupation listed

question: Comment on the statement that elements of the first transition series possess many properties different from those of heavier transition elements.
solution: The first-row (3d) transition elements differ from the heavier (4d, 5d) series in several ways: (1) They show a greater tendency to form high-spin complexes and paramagnetic compounds, since their 3d orbitals are more contracted/less diffuse and produce weaker ligand fields with common ligands compared to more diffuse 4d/5d orbitals which favour low-spin, strong-field complexes. (2) Metal–metal bonding is weaker/less common in the first series (e.g. Cr, Mn) compared to extensive metal-metal bonding in 2nd/3rd row congeners (e.g. Mo, W, Re clusters). (3) 3d metals generally show lower maximum oxidation states than their heavier congeners in the same group (e.g. Mn maximum +7 vs Tc/Re commonly +7 too but more stably; Fe max +6 vs Ru/Os reaching +8). (4) Enthalpies of atomisation of the 3d series are generally lower than those of the 4d/5d series, so 3d metals are somewhat softer/lower melting on average. (5) Catalytic properties, magnetic behaviour and colour intensities also differ due to differences in crystal field splitting energies (3d complexes have smaller Δo than analogous 4d/5d complexes).
steps: 3d orbitals are more compact/less diffuse than 4d/5d, leading to weaker orbital overlap with ligands and smaller crystal field splitting — hence more high-spin, paramagnetic complexes in 1st-row chemistry
Heavier congeners show more extensive metal-metal bonding and easier access to very high oxidation states (e.g. Os +8) compared to 1st row analogues
First-row elements generally have lower enthalpies of atomisation and different catalytic/magnetic behaviour compared to 4d/5d congeners

question:
What can be inferred from the magnetic moment values of the following complex species?
K4[Mn(CN)6]: Magnetic Moment = 2.2 BM
[Fe(H2O)6]2+: Magnetic Moment = 5.3 BM
K2[MnCl4]: Magnetic Moment = 5.9 BM
solution:
K4[Mn(CN)6]: Mn is in +2 state (3d⁵); observed μ=2.2 BM corresponds to n≈1 unpaired electron, meaning CN⁻ (a strong field ligand) causes maximum pairing, giving a low-spin d2sp3 (inner orbital, octahedral) complex.
[Fe(H2O)6]2+: Fe is +2 (3d⁶); μ=5.3 BM corresponds to n≈4 unpaired electrons, meaning H2O (weak field ligand) does not cause pairing, giving a high-spin sp3d2 (outer orbital) complex.
K2[MnCl4]: Mn is +2 (3d⁵); μ=5.9 BM corresponds to n≈5 unpaired electrons (all d-electrons unpaired), meaning Cl⁻ (weak field ligand) causes no pairing, giving a high-spin, tetrahedral (sp3) complex.
steps: Use spin-only formula μ=√(n(n+2)) to back-calculate n (number of unpaired electrons) from each given magnetic moment

Compare n with the maximum possible unpaired electrons for the free ion's d-count (Mn²⁺=3d⁵ max 5 unpaired; Fe²⁺=3d⁶ max 4 unpaired) to decide if the ligand (CN⁻ strong field vs H2O/Cl⁻ weak field) has caused electron pairing (low spin) or not (high spin)
Mn(CN)6⁴⁻: n=1 ≪ 5 ⇒ strong-field CN⁻ causes pairing ⇒ low-spin d2sp3 complex
Fe(H2O)6²⁺: n=4 (matches max for high-spin d6) ⇒ weak-field H2O, no pairing ⇒ high-spin sp3d2 complex
MnCl4²⁻: n=5 (matches max for high-spin d5) ⇒ weak-field Cl⁻, no pairing, and stoichiometry [MnCl4]²⁻ suggests tetrahedral sp3 geometry

question: Explain the bonding in coordination compounds in terms of Werner's postulates.
solution: Werner's postulates (1893) explain coordination compound bonding as follows: (1) Metals possess two types of valency — primary (ionisable, satisfied by negative ions, corresponds to the oxidation state) and secondary (non-ionisable, satisfied by neutral or negative ligands, corresponds to the coordination number, and is fixed/characteristic for the metal). (2) Every metal atom/ion has a fixed number of secondary valencies (coordination number), e.g. 6 or 4, and these are directed in space in fixed geometric arrangements (octahedral for CN 6, tetrahedral or square planar for CN 4), giving coordination compounds their definite geometry. (3) The primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied usually by negative ions; secondary valencies are non-ionisable, always satisfied by the same fixed number of ligands (neutral molecules like NH3, H2O or negative ions), and point in definite directions, explaining stereoisomerism in complexes. This model correctly predicted properties like the number of ions produced on dissociation, and the existence of geometric/optical isomers of complexes.
steps: Primary valency = ionisable valency, equal to the oxidation state, satisfied by anions that can dissociate in solution
Secondary valency = non-ionisable, fixed coordination number, satisfied by ligands directly bonded to the metal in a fixed spatial arrangement
Fixed spatial (geometric) arrangement of secondary valencies (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar) explains the shape and isomerism of complexes

question: FeSO4 solution mixed with (NH4)2SO4 solution in 1:1 molar ratio gives the test of Fe2+ ion but CuSO4 solution mixed with aqueous ammonia in 1:4 molar ratio does not give the test of Cu2+ ion. Explain why?
solution: FeSO4 and (NH4)2SO4 in 1:1 ratio form a double salt, Mohr's salt, FeSO4·(NH4)2SO4·6H2O, which dissociates completely in solution into its constituent simple ions (Fe²⁺, NH4⁺, SO4²⁻), so free Fe²⁺ ions are available and give the usual Fe²⁺ test. In contrast, CuSO4 with excess aqueous ammonia (1:4 ratio) forms a coordination complex, [Cu(NH3)4]SO4 (tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate), in which Cu²⁺ is bound to the four NH3 ligands through coordinate bonds forming a complex ion [Cu(NH3)4]²⁺ that does not dissociate significantly in solution to release free Cu²⁺ ions; hence the usual test for Cu²⁺ is not obtained.
steps: Distinguish a double salt (dissociates fully into simple ions in solution) from a coordination compound (forms a stable complex ion that does not release the simple metal ion significantly)
FeSO4·(NH4)2SO4 (Mohr's salt) is a double salt → free Fe²⁺ present → gives Fe²⁺ test
[Cu(NH3)4]SO4 is a coordination compound → Cu²⁺ locked up in the stable complex ion [Cu(NH3)4]²⁺ → no free Cu²⁺ → no Cu²⁺ test

question: Explain with two examples each of the following: coordination entity, ligand, coordination number, coordination polyhedron, homoleptic and heteroleptic.
solution:
Coordination entity: a central metal atom/ion bonded to a fixed number of ions/molecules, e.g. [Co(NH3)6]³⁺, [PtCl4]²⁻.
Ligand: an ion or molecule directly attached to the central metal atom, e.g. Cl⁻, NH3 (also en, CN⁻ etc.).
Coordination number: the number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal, e.g. in [PtCl6]²⁻ CN=6; in [Ni(CN)4]²⁻ CN=4.
Coordination polyhedron: the spatial arrangement of the ligand atoms directly attached to the central atom, e.g. octahedral in [Co(NH3)6]³⁺, tetrahedral in [Ni(CO)4].
Homoleptic: complexes in which the metal is bound to only one kind of donor group, e.g. [Co(NH3)6]³⁺, [Fe(CN)6]³⁻.
Heteroleptic: complexes in which the metal is bound to more than one kind of donor group, e.g. [Co(NH3)4Cl2]⁺, [Ni(NH3)4Cl2].
steps: For each term, give the definition as per NCERT and pick two well-known example complexes that illustrate it
Coordination entity/ligand/coordination number/coordination polyhedron describe structural features of a complex
Homoleptic (one kind of ligand) vs heteroleptic (mixed ligands) classify complexes by ligand variety

question: What is meant by unidentate, didentate and ambidentate ligands? Give two examples for each.
solution:
Unidentate (monodentate) ligand: binds to the metal through only one donor atom, e.g. Cl⁻, NH3, H2O, CN⁻.
Didentate (bidentate) ligand: has two donor atoms, both of which bind simultaneously to the metal, e.g. ethylenediamine (en, H2NCH2CH2NH2), oxalate ion (C2O4²⁻).
Ambidentate ligand: a ligand with two different donor atoms, but only one of which coordinates to the metal at a time (either atom can bind, giving linkage isomers), e.g. thiocyanate (SCN⁻, can bind through S or N), nitrite (NO2⁻, can bind through N as nitro or O as nitrito).
steps: Unidentate: one donor atom binds — e.g. NH3, Cl⁻
Didentate: two donor atoms bind simultaneously (chelating) — e.g. en, oxalate
Ambidentate: two possible donor atoms, but only one binds at a time (either atom, giving isomers) — e.g. SCN⁻, NO2⁻

Specify the oxidation numbers of the metals in the following coordination entities:
(i) [Co(H2O)(CN)(en)2]2+
