question: List various types of isomerism possible for coordination compounds, giving an example of each.
solution: Coordination compounds show two broad classes of isomerism: (A) Stereoisomerism — (1) Geometrical isomerism, e.g. cis- and trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]; (2) Optical isomerism, e.g. cis-[PtCl2(en)2]²⁺ exists as non-superimposable mirror-image (d and l) forms. (B) Structural isomerism — (1) Linkage isomerism, e.g. [Co(NH3)5(NO2)]²⁺ (nitro, N-bonded) vs [Co(NH3)5(ONO)]²⁺ (nitrito, O-bonded); (2) Coordination isomerism, e.g. [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] vs [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]; (3) Ionisation isomerism, e.g. [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 vs [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br; (4) Solvate (hydrate) isomerism, e.g. [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 vs [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O.
steps: Group isomerism types under stereoisomerism (same bonds, different spatial arrangement: geometrical, optical) and structural isomerism (different bonds/connectivity: linkage, coordination, ionisation, solvate)
Provide the standard textbook example for each type

question:
How many geometrical isomers are possible in the following coordination entities?
(i) [Cr(C2O4)3]3–
(ii) [Co(NH3)3Cl3]
solution:
(i) [Cr(C2O4)3]³⁻: nil — no geometrical isomers are possible (oxalate is a symmetric bidentate ligand and all three chelate rings are equivalent in an octahedral tris-chelate, so only optical isomers, not geometrical, occur here).
(ii) [Co(NH3)3Cl3]: two geometrical isomers are possible — facial (fac, three Cl's on one triangular face) and meridional (mer, three Cl's along a meridian).
steps: (i) A symmetric tris(bidentate) octahedral complex like [M(AA)3] has only one possible arrangement (all three chelate rings equivalent), so no geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism, though optical (d/l) isomerism is possible
(ii) An MA3B3-type octahedral complex ([Co(NH3)3Cl3]) has exactly two possible geometric arrangements: fac (3 like groups on one face) and mer (3 like groups in a meridional plane)

question:
Draw the structures of optical isomers of:
(i) [Cr(C2O4)3]3–
(ii) [PtCl2(en)2]2+
(iii) [Cr(NH3)2Cl2(en)]+
solution:
(i) [Cr(C2O4)3]³⁻ (a tris-chelate octahedral complex with 3 symmetric bidentate oxalate ligands) exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (Δ and Λ enantiomers), like a three-bladed propeller twisted in opposite senses.
(ii) cis-[PtCl2(en)2]²⁺ (the cis isomer, with the two Cl's adjacent) is chiral and exists as d and l optical isomers (mirror images); the trans isomer is achiral (has a plane of symmetry) and shows no optical isomerism.
(iii) cis-[Cr(NH3)2Cl2(en)]⁺ is chiral and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror-image optical isomers; the trans isomer is achiral.
steps: Optical isomerism arises in octahedral complexes that lack an internal plane of symmetry (chiral), most commonly in cis-isomers of complexes containing chelating (bidentate) ligands
(i) The tris(oxalato) complex is inherently chiral (propeller-like Δ/Λ arrangement) regardless of any 'cis/trans' label, since all three bidentate ligands are equivalent

(ii)&(iii) Only the cis-form (where the two like monodentate/simple ligands are adjacent, disrupting any mirror plane) is chiral and gives d/l optical isomers; the trans-form has a mirror plane and is optically inactive

question:
Draw all the isomers (geometrical and optical) of:
(i) [CoCl2(en)2]+
(ii) [Co(NH3)Cl(en)2]2+
(iii) [Co(NH3)2Cl2(en)]+
solution:
(i) [CoCl2(en)2]⁺: two geometrical isomers, cis and trans. Trans is optically inactive (has a mirror plane); cis is chiral and exists as a pair of optical isomers (cis-d and cis-l). Total: 3 isomers (trans, cis-d, cis-l).
(ii) [Co(NH3)Cl(en)2]²⁺: two geometrical isomers, cis and trans. Trans is achiral; cis is chiral, giving cis-d and cis-l. Total: 3 isomers.
(iii) [Co(NH3)2Cl2(en)]⁺: two geometrical isomers, cis and trans. Both cis and trans forms of this complex are chiral in principle, but conventionally (as per NCERT) the trans form is considered to have a plane of symmetry through the en ligand and is optically inactive, while the cis form is chiral, giving cis-d and cis-l. Total: 3 isomers.
steps: For [M(AA)2B2]-type octahedral complexes (2 bidentate + 2 different monodentate ligands), cis and trans geometrical isomers exist
Trans isomer generally possesses an internal mirror plane (achiral, optically inactive); cis isomer usually lacks this symmetry and is chiral, giving a d and l pair
Apply this pattern to each of the three given complexes to enumerate cis (chiral, 2 optical forms) + trans (1 achiral form) = 3 total isomers each

question: Write all the geometrical isomers of [Pt(NH3)(Br)(Cl)(py)] and how many of these will exhibit optical isomers?
solution: [Pt(NH3)(Br)(Cl)(py)] is a square planar complex of the type MABCD (four different ligands). It has three possible geometrical isomers, depending on which pair of ligands is placed trans to each other: (NH3 trans to Br, with Cl trans to py), (NH3 trans to Cl, with Br trans to py), and (NH3 trans to py, with Br trans to Cl). None of these three geometrical isomers exhibit optical isomerism, because square planar complexes (being essentially two-dimensional/planar) always possess a plane of symmetry (the molecular plane itself), so they are achiral.
steps: Square planar MABCD complexes have 3 possible geometric arrangements based on which ligand pairs sit trans to each other (3 = 4!/(2×2×2), accounting for symmetry)
Square planar complexes are inherently planar and achiral (the plane of the complex is itself a mirror plane), so none show optical isomerism, regardless of how many different ligands are present

question:
Aqueous copper sulphate solution (blue in colour) gives:
(i) a green precipitate with aqueous potassium fluoride and
(ii) a bright green solution with aqueous potassium chloride. Explain these experimental results.
solution:
Aqueous CuSO4 exists as the blue [Cu(H2O)4]²⁺ complex ion. (i) When KF is added, the weakly-bound H2O ligands are displaced by the smaller, more strongly-bound F⁻ ligands, forming the green, relatively insoluble complex [CuF4]²⁻ (precipitates as a green solid): [Cu(H2O)4]²⁺ + 4F⁻ → [CuF4]²⁻ + 4H2O.
(ii) When KCl is added, the weak H2O ligands are similarly replaced by Cl⁻ ligands to give the soluble bright green complex ion [CuCl4]²⁻: [Cu(H2O)4]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ → [CuCl4]²⁻ + 4H2O.
steps: Aqueous Cu²⁺ exists as the blue tetraaqua complex [Cu(H2O)4]²⁺
F⁻ and Cl⁻ are both able to displace the weakly bound H2O ligands, forming new tetrahalido complexes with different colours
[CuF4]²⁻ is a green, sparingly soluble precipitate; [CuCl4]²⁻ is a bright green species that stays in solution

question: What is the coordination entity formed when excess of aqueous KCN is added to an aqueous solution of copper sulphate? Why is it that no precipitate of copper sulphide is obtained when H2S(g) is passed through this solution?
solution: Excess aqueous KCN reacts with CuSO4 to form the very stable complex ion [Cu(CN)4]²⁻ (tetracyanidocuprate(II) ion, which can further get reduced to the Cu(I) complex [Cu(CN)4]³⁻ with release of cyanogen, but the immediate complex formed is [Cu(CN)4]²⁻/[Cu(CN)4]³⁻ type): [Cu(H2O)4]²⁺ + 4CN⁻ → [Cu(CN)4]²⁻ + 4H2O. Since CN⁻ is a very strong ligand, this complex is extremely stable (very high formation constant), so the concentration of free Cu²⁺ ions in solution becomes extremely small. When H2S is passed, the low concentration of free Cu²⁺ is insufficient to exceed the solubility product of CuS, so no precipitate of copper sulphide forms.
steps: CN⁻ (strong ligand) displaces water from [Cu(H2O)4]²⁺, forming the very stable cyanide complex [Cu(CN)4]²⁻ (and related species)
The high stability constant of this complex means [Cu²⁺]free is vanishingly small
Since the ionic product [Cu²⁺][S²⁻] cannot exceed the very small Ksp of CuS at this tiny free Cu²⁺ concentration, no CuS precipitate forms

question:
Discuss the nature of bonding in the following coordination entities on the basis of valence bond theory:
(i) [Fe(CN)6]3–
(ii) [Fe(H2O)6]4–[typo, actually 2+ from context—kept per book pairing with [FeF6]3– and [Co(C2O4)3]3–, [CoF6]3–]
(iii) [Co(C2O4)3]3–
(iv) [CoF6]3–
solution:
(i) [Fe(CN)6]³⁻: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵; CN⁻ is a strong field ligand, causing pairing of the 5 d-electrons into the three lower t2g orbitals, leaving two d-orbitals free for d2sp3 hybridisation — an inner orbital, octahedral, low-spin complex with 1 unpaired electron (paramagnetic, weakly).
(ii) [Fe(H2O)6]... (analogous case, e.g. [FeF6]³⁻): Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵; F⁻ (and H2O for the corresponding Fe²⁺ complex) is a weak field ligand, so the 5 (or 6) d-electrons remain unpaired, using sp3d2 hybridisation with the outer 4d orbitals — an outer orbital, octahedral, high-spin complex with maximum unpaired electrons (strongly paramagnetic).
(iii) [Co(C2O4)3]³⁻: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶; oxalate is a moderately strong chelating ligand that causes pairing of the 6 d-electrons into t2g, leaving two d-orbitals free for d2sp3 hybridisation — an inner orbital, octahedral, diamagnetic (low-spin, 0 unpaired electrons) complex.
(iv) [CoF6]³⁻: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶; F⁻ is a weak field ligand, so pairing does not occur, and sp3d2 hybridisation (outer orbital complex) is used, giving 4 unpaired electrons (strongly paramagnetic, high-spin).
steps: Determine the metal's oxidation state and d-electron count, then classify each ligand as weak-field (does not force pairing, e.g. F⁻, H2O) or strong-field (forces pairing, e.g. CN⁻, oxalate for Co)
Strong-field ligand → electrons pair up in existing (n-1)d orbitals → inner orbital complex using d2sp3 hybrid orbitals, low spin, fewer unpaired electrons
Weak-field ligand → electrons remain unpaired, following Hund's rule → outer orbital complex using sp3d2 hybrid orbitals (involving the higher nd orbitals), high spin, more unpaired electrons
Apply this to each of the four complexes based on the given ligand identity to get the hybridisation, orbital type and magnetic behaviour

question: Draw figure to show the splitting of d orbitals in an octahedral crystal field.
solution: In an octahedral crystal field, the five originally degenerate d-orbitals split into two sets: a lower-energy triply-degenerate set called t2g (comprising dxy, dyz, dzx, which point between the ligand-along-axes directions and experience less repulsion) and a higher-energy doubly-degenerate set called eg (comprising dz² and dx²−y², which point directly at the six ligands along the axes and experience greater repulsion). The energy gap between the eg and t2g sets is called the crystal field splitting energy, Δo (or 10Dq); the eg set lies 0.6Δo above, and the t2g set lies 0.4Δo below, the original (barycentre) energy level of the unsplit d-orbitals.
steps: Octahedral field: ligands approach along the ±x, ±y, ±z axes
Orbitals pointing along axes (dz², dx²−y²) face direct ligand repulsion — raised in energy — forming the eg (doubly degenerate) set, at +0.6Δo
Orbitals pointing between the axes (dxy, dyz, dxz) are less repelled — lowered in energy — forming the t2g (triply degenerate) set, at −0.4Δo
The energy difference between eg and t2g is the crystal field splitting energy Δo (10Dq)

question: What is spectrochemical series? Explain the difference between a weak field ligand and a strong field ligand.
solution: The spectrochemical series is the arrangement of common ligands in order of their increasing crystal-field-splitting ability (increasing Δo), determined experimentally from the electronic spectra of their metal complexes: I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < N3⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C2O4²⁻ < H2O < NCS⁻ < py ≈ NH3 < en < NO2⁻(as N-bonded, nitro) < CN⁻ < CO. A weak field ligand produces only a small crystal field splitting (Δo), so it is unable to force pairing of electrons in the lower t2g set; electrons instead remain unpaired (Hund's rule dominates), giving high-spin complexes with more unpaired electrons (e.g. F⁻, Cl⁻, H2O). A strong field ligand produces a large crystal field splitting, large enough to overcome the pairing energy, so electrons preferentially pair up in the lower t2g orbitals rather than occupy the higher eg orbitals singly, giving low-spin complexes with fewer unpaired electrons (e.g. CN⁻, CO, NO2⁻).
steps: Spectrochemical series = experimentally-derived ordering of ligands by their ability to split d-orbitals (Δo), from weakest to strongest field
Weak field ligands (I⁻,Br⁻,Cl⁻,F⁻,H2O...) give small Δo < pairing energy P ⇒ high-spin complexes (Hund's rule obeyed, max unpaired electrons)
Strong field ligands (CN⁻,CO,NO2⁻...) give large Δo > pairing energy P ⇒ low-spin complexes (electrons pair up in t2g before occupying eg)

question: What is crystal field splitting energy? How does the magnitude of Δo decide the actual configuration of d orbitals in a coordination entity?
solution: Crystal field splitting energy (Δo for octahedral fields) is the energy difference between the higher-energy eg set and the lower-energy t2g set of d-orbitals, created when a spherically symmetric field of ligand negative charges is replaced by the actual octahedral arrangement of ligands, causing unequal electrostatic repulsion on the differently-oriented d-orbitals. For configurations d⁴ to d⁷ in an octahedral field, the actual electron arrangement depends on the relative magnitude of Δo compared to the pairing energy P: if Δo < P (weak field ligands), it costs less energy for the 4th (or subsequent) electron to enter the higher eg orbital than to pair up in t2g, so electrons remain unpaired as far as possible — giving a high-spin configuration. If Δo > P (strong field ligands), it costs less energy for electrons to pair up in the lower t2g set than to be promoted to eg, giving a low-spin configuration.
steps: Δo = energy gap created between t2g and eg sets when a metal ion is placed in an octahedral ligand field
For d⁴–d⁷ ions, there is a choice for the 'extra' electron(s): pair up in t2g (cost = pairing energy P) or occupy eg singly (cost = Δo)
If Δo < P (weak field): electron goes to eg unpaired → high-spin configuration
If Δo > P (strong field): electron pairs in t2g → low-spin configuration

question: [Cr(NH3)6]3+ is paramagnetic while [Ni(CN)4]2– is diamagnetic. Explain why?
solution: In [Cr(NH3)6]³⁺, Cr³⁺ is 3d³; regardless of ligand field strength, all three electrons occupy the t2g orbitals singly (Hund's rule, no pairing needed/possible since there are exactly 3 orbitals for 3 electrons), giving 3 unpaired electrons, so the complex is paramagnetic. In [Ni(CN)4]²⁻, Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸; CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand that causes the complex to adopt a square planar geometry via dsp2 hybridisation — this requires pairing up all the d-electrons (using one d-orbital, dx²−y², in the hybridisation) so that all 8 electrons in the remaining d-orbitals are paired, leaving zero unpaired electrons, making the complex diamagnetic.
steps: Cr³⁺ (3d³): exactly 3 electrons fill the 3 t2g orbitals singly (unavoidably unpaired) regardless of field strength → paramagnetic

Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) with strong-field CN⁻: adopts square planar geometry via dsp2 hybridisation, requiring the dx²−y² orbital to be empty, which forces full pairing of all 8 d-electrons in the remaining four d-orbitals → diamagnetic

question: A solution of [Ni(H2O)6]2+ is green but a solution of [Ni(CN)4]2– is colourless. Explain.
solution: [Ni(H2O)6]²⁺: Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸; H2O is a weak field ligand giving an octahedral, high-spin, sp3d2 complex with unpaired electrons in partially-filled d-orbitals (eg has 2 unpaired electrons). This allows d-d electronic transitions on absorption of visible light, and the complementary colour (green) of the absorbed light is observed. [Ni(CN)4]²⁻: with strong-field CN⁻ ligands, Ni²⁺ forms a square planar, diamagnetic, dsp2 complex in which all d-orbitals (including dx²−y² which is vacated for hybridisation) are either fully occupied (paired) or completely empty — there is a large energy gap and no partially-filled d-orbital set available for a low-energy d-d transition in the visible region; the transition instead requires much higher (often UV-range) energy, so no visible light is absorbed and the complex appears colourless.
steps: Colour depends on whether a low-energy d-d transition is available within the visible light energy range, which requires partially-filled (not fully empty or fully paired-up-into-nonexistence) d-orbital sets with an appropriate splitting energy
[Ni(H2O)6]²⁺ (octahedral, high-spin) has a normal d-d transition in the visible range → coloured (green)
[Ni(CN)4]²⁻ (square planar, diamagnetic, using dsp2 hybridisation) has all electrons paired with a much larger HOMO-LUMO type gap not matching visible light → colourless

question: [Fe(CN)6]4– and [Fe(H2O)6]2+ are of different colours in dilute solutions. Why?
solution: Both complexes have Fe²⁺ (3d⁶), but the ligands CN⁻ and H2O differ greatly in field strength (position in the spectrochemical series), so they produce very different crystal field splitting energies (Δo). Since the colour observed corresponds to the complementary colour of the specific wavelength of visible light absorbed for the d-d transition, and the transition energy equals Δo (which differs for the two complexes), the two complexes absorb different wavelengths of light and therefore appear differently coloured.
steps: Both are Fe²⁺(3d⁶) complexes, so the difference in colour must come from the ligand, not the metal ion
CN⁻ (strong field) gives a large Δo; H2O (weak field) gives a much smaller Δo
Since absorbed photon energy = Δo (for the d-d transition), different Δo values mean different absorbed wavelengths, hence different observed (complementary) colours

question: Discuss the nature of bonding in metal carbonyls.
solution: The metal–carbon bond in metal carbonyls possesses both σ and π character. (1) A σ-bond is formed by the donation of the lone pair of electrons on the carbon atom of CO into a vacant hybrid orbital of the metal (a simple ligand-to-metal donor bond). (2) Simultaneously, a π-bond is formed by the back-donation ('back bonding') of electron density from a filled metal d-orbital (of appropriate symmetry) into the vacant antibonding π* orbital of the CO ligand. This synergic combination of σ-donation (ligand→metal) and π-back-donation (metal→ligand) strengthens the metal–carbon bond and simultaneously weakens the C–O bond (since electron density enters the C–O antibonding orbital), which is why the C–O bond in carbonyls is longer/weaker (lower stretching frequency in IR) than in free CO gas, while the M–C bond acquires partial double-bond character.
steps: The M–CO bond is a synergic combination of two components acting together
σ-donation: lone pair on C of CO donates into an empty metal orbital
π-back-donation: filled metal d-orbital donates electron density into the empty π* antibonding orbital of CO
This synergic bonding strengthens the M–C bond (partial double bond character) while weakening the C≡O bond compared to free CO

question:
Give the oxidation state, d orbital occupation and coordination number of the central metal ion in the following complexes:
(i) K3[Co(C2O4)3]
(ii) cis-[CrCl2(en)2]Cl
(iii) (NH4)2[CoF4]
(iv) [Mn(H2O)6]SO4
solution:
(i) K3[Co(C2O4)3]: Co oxidation state +3, d-configuration 3d⁶ (t2g⁶ eg⁰ as low spin, oxalate being strong-field-ish here), coordination number 6.
(ii) cis-[CrCl2(en)2]Cl: Cr oxidation state +3, d-configuration 3d³ (t2g³), coordination number 6.
(iii) (NH4)2[CoF4]: Co oxidation state +2, d-configuration 3d⁷ (t2g⁵ eg² high spin, tetrahedral), coordination number 4.
(iv) [Mn(H2O)6]SO4: Mn oxidation state +2, d-configuration 3d⁵ (t2g³ eg² high spin), coordination number 6.
steps: For each complex, determine the metal oxidation state by balancing ligand charges against the overall charge/counter-ion charge, then note the coordination number from the number of donor atoms, and derive d-electron count from the periodic group number minus the oxidation state
(i) 3K⁺ balances [Co(C2O4)3]³⁻; oxalate²⁻×3=−6; Co+(−6)=−3 ⇒ Co=+3, d⁶, CN=6
(ii) 1Cl⁻ counter-ion balances [CrCl2(en)2]⁺; en=0, Cl⁻(coordinated)×2=−2; Cr+(−2)=+1 ⇒ Cr=+3, d³, CN=6
(iii) 2NH4⁺ balances [CoF4]²⁻; F⁻×4=−4; Co+(−4)=−2 ⇒ Co=+2, d⁷, CN=4
(iv) SO4²⁻ balances [Mn(H2O)6]²⁺; H2O=0; Mn=+2, d⁵, CN=6

question:
Write down the IUPAC name for each of the following complexes and indicate the oxidation state, electronic configuration and coordination number. Also give stereochemistry and magnetic moment of the complex:
(i) K[Cr(H2O)2(C2O4)2].3H2O
(ii) [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2
(iii) CrCl3(py)3
(iv) Cs[FeCl4]
(v) K4[Mn(CN)6]
solution:
(i) Potassium diaquabis(oxalato)chromate(III) trihydrate. Cr: +3, 3d³, CN=6, octahedral, μ = √15 = 3.87 BM (3 unpaired electrons).
(ii) Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride. Co: +3, 3d⁶, CN=6, octahedral, low-spin, diamagnetic (μ≈0).
(iii) Trichloridotris(pyridine)chromium(III). Cr: +3, 3d³, CN=6, octahedral, μ=3.87 BM.
(iv) Caesium tetrachloridoferrate(III). Fe: +3, 3d⁵, CN=4, tetrahedral, high-spin, μ=5.92 BM (5 unpaired electrons).
(v) Potassium hexacyanidomanganate(II). Mn: +2, 3d⁵, CN=6, octahedral, low-spin (CN⁻ strong field), μ = √3 = 1.73 BM (1 unpaired electron).
steps: For each complex: name per IUPAC rules; find oxidation state by charge balance; get d-electron count; note CN and expected geometry (6→octahedral, 4→tetrahedral, unless noted square planar)
Decide high-spin vs low-spin based on ligand field strength (CN⁻ strong-field, halides/H2O/py weak-field for these metals), and compute unpaired electrons accordingly
Magnetic moment via spin-only formula μ=√(n(n+2)) BM using the resulting n

question: Explain the violet colour of the complex [Ti(H2O)6]3+ on the basis of crystal field theory.
solution: In [Ti(H2O)6]³⁺, Ti³⁺ has a single 3d electron (3d¹). In the octahedral field of the six weak-field H2O ligands, the d-orbitals split into the lower t2g set and higher eg set, and the single electron occupies a t2g orbital in the ground state. On absorbing light of appropriate energy (in the visible region, corresponding to Δo), this electron is excited from the t2g to the eg level (a d-d transition). The complex absorbs light in the yellow-green region of the visible spectrum to bring about this transition, and the light that is transmitted (the complementary colour, violet) is what is observed, giving the complex its characteristic violet colour.
steps: Ti³⁺ is 3d¹, so in the octahedral aqua-complex the single electron sits in a t2g orbital in the ground state
Absorption of a visible-light photon (matching Δo) promotes this electron t2g→eg (a d-d transition)
The complex absorbs yellow-green light for this transition, and the complementary transmitted colour (violet) is what we observe

question: What is meant by the chelate effect? Give an example.
solution: The chelate effect refers to the enhanced thermodynamic stability of a metal complex containing chelating (polydentate) ligands compared to an analogous complex with a similar number of comparable monodentate ligands, mainly due to the favourable entropy change (release of more free ligand/solvent molecules) when a chelate ring forms. For example, [Ni(en)3]²⁺ (with three bidentate ethylenediamine ligands) is significantly more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]²⁺ (with six monodentate ammonia ligands), even though the immediate donor atoms and overall coordination number (6, N-donors) are essentially the same in both.
steps: Chelate effect = extra stability gained when a polydentate (chelating) ligand replaces an equivalent number of monodentate ligands, mainly due to a favourable entropy increase upon complex formation (more free small molecules released per chelate ring closed)
Example: [Ni(en)3]²⁺ is more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]²⁺

question:
Discuss briefly giving an example in each case the role of coordination compounds in:
(i) biological systems
(ii) medicinal chemistry and
(iii) analytical chemistry
(iv) extraction/metallurgy of metals.
solution:
(i) Biological systems: Many biologically essential molecules are metal coordination complexes, e.g. haemoglobin (an iron-porphyrin complex) which transports O2 in blood, and chlorophyll (a magnesium-porphyrin complex) essential for photosynthesis in plants; vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) is a cobalt complex.
(ii) Medicinal chemistry: Coordination compounds are used as drugs, e.g. cisplatin, cis-[PtCl2(NH3)2], is used as an anticancer drug; EDTA is used as a chelating agent to treat lead (and other heavy metal) poisoning by forming a stable, excretable metal-EDTA complex.
(iii) Analytical chemistry: Coordination compounds are used in qualitative and quantitative analysis, e.g. formation of coloured complexes for identification/estimation of metal ions — Ni²⁺ is estimated gravimetrically as the red complex with dimethylglyoxime (DMG); EDTA titrations are used to estimate hardness of water (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺).
(iv) Extraction/metallurgy of metals: Coordination compounds play a role in extraction, e.g. gold and silver are extracted from their ores by forming soluble cyanide complexes, [Au(CN)2]⁻ and [Ag(CN)2]⁻, from which the pure metal is later recovered by displacement with zinc; purification of nickel is done via formation and thermal decomposition of the volatile complex Ni(CO)4 (Mond process).
steps: (i) Metal-porphyrin/corrin complexes essential to life: haemoglobin (Fe), chlorophyll (Mg), vitamin B12 (Co)
(ii) Drugs based on coordination chemistry: cisplatin as anticancer agent; EDTA as antidote/chelation therapy for heavy metal poisoning
(iii) Analytical use: coloured/characteristic complexes for qualitative tests (Ni-DMG) and quantitative titrations (EDTA for water hardness)
(iv) Metallurgical extraction/purification via complex formation: cyanide complexes for Au/Ag extraction, Mond process (Ni(CO)4) for nickel purification

question:
How many ions are produced from the complex Co(NH3)6Cl2 in solution?
(i) 6 (ii) 4 (iii) 3 (iv) 2
solution: (iii) 3 ions.
steps: The complex is [Co(NH3)6]Cl2 (with NH3 as neutral ligands coordinated to Co, and Cl⁻ as ionisable counter-ions)
In solution it dissociates as [Co(NH3)6]Cl2 → [Co(NH3)6]²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, giving a total of 1 + 2 = 3 ions

question:
Amongst the following ions which one has the highest magnetic moment value?
(i) [Cr(H2O)6]3+
(ii) [Fe(H2O)6]2+
(iii) [Zn(H2O)6]2+
solution: (ii) [Fe(H2O)6]²⁺ has the highest magnetic moment.
steps: Cr³⁺ = 3d³ → 3 unpaired electrons (high spin, weak field H2O) → μ=√(3×5)=3.87 BM
Fe²⁺ = 3d⁶ → in weak field H2O, high spin, 4 unpaired electrons → μ=√(4×6)=4.90 BM
Zn²⁺ = 3d¹⁰ → 0 unpaired electrons → μ=0 (diamagnetic)
Comparing 3.87, 4.90 and 0 BM, Fe²⁺ (ii) has the highest magnetic moment

question:
Amongst the following, the most stable complex is
(i) [Fe(H2O)6]3+
(ii) [Fe(NH3)6]3+
(iii) [Fe(C2O4)3]3–
(iv) [FeCl6]3–
solution: (iii) [Fe(C2O4)3]³⁻ is the most stable complex.
steps: Stability of complexes generally increases with the chelate effect (bidentate/polydentate ligands give more stable complexes than monodentate ligands of comparable donor strength)
Among the given ligands (H2O, NH3, oxalate (bidentate), Cl⁻), only oxalate is a chelating (bidentate) ligand
The chelate effect makes [Fe(C2O4)3]³⁻ significantly more thermodynamically stable than the other monodentate-ligand complexes

question:
What will be the correct order for the wavelengths of absorption in the visible region for the following:
[Ni(NO2)6]4–, [Ni(NH3)6]2+, [Ni(H2O)6]2+ ?
solution: Order of absorbed wavelength (increasing): [Ni(NO2)6]⁴⁻ < [Ni(NH3)6]²⁺ < [Ni(H2O)6]²⁺.
steps: In the spectrochemical series, ligand field strength (and hence Δo) follows: H2O < NH3 < NO2⁻ (nitro, N-bonded)
Since Δo (energy absorbed for the d-d transition) increases in the order H2O < NH3 < NO2⁻, the absorbed photon energy increases in that order too

Since wavelength is inversely proportional to energy (E=hc/λ), the order of absorbed wavelengths is the reverse: [Ni(NO2)6]⁴⁻ (highest Δo, shortest λ) < [Ni(NH3)6]²⁺ < [Ni(H2O)6]²⁺ (lowest Δo, longest λ)
