(2) Propanal (nucleophile) + butanal (electrophile): CH3CH2CH(OH)CH(CH3)CHO with the extra carbon from butanal → 2-methyl-3-hydroxyhexanal.
(3) Butanal (nucleophile) + butanal (electrophile): CH3CH2CH2CH(OH)CH(C2H5)CHO → 2-ethyl-3-hydroxyhexanal.
(4) Butanal (nucleophile) + propanal (electrophile): CH3CH2CH(OH)CH(C2H5)CHO → 2-ethyl-3-hydroxypentanal.
steps: A crossed (mixed) aldol reaction between two different aldehydes, each possessing α-hydrogens, can give 4 products since either aldehyde can act as the nucleophile (forming the enolate at its α-carbon, which attacks) while the other acts as the electrophile (its carbonyl carbon being attacked)
Pairing propanal-as-nucleophile with propanal-as-electrophile and with butanal-as-electrophile, and likewise for butanal-as-nucleophile, gives the 4 combinations/products listed
In each product, the carbon skeleton reflects: [nucleophile's α-carbon]–CH(OH)–[electrophile's original carbonyl carbon, now bearing OH after protonation]–[rest of electrophile chain]

question: An organic compound with the molecular formula C9H10O forms 2,4-DNP derivative, reduces Tollens' reagent and undergoes Cannizzaro reaction. On vigorous oxidation, it gives 1,2-benzenedicarboxylic acid. Identify the compound.
solution: The compound is 2-ethylbenzaldehyde (o-ethylbenzaldehyde), C6H4(C2H5)(CHO)-ortho.
steps: Formation of 2,4-DNP derivative + reduction of Tollens' reagent confirms the compound is an aldehyde
Undergoing the Cannizzaro reaction confirms it has NO α-hydrogen, i.e. it is an aromatic (or otherwise non-enolisable) aldehyde, ArCHO

Vigorous oxidation giving 1,2-benzenedicarboxylic acid (phthalic acid) means the benzene ring bears two oxidisable side chains at ortho positions that both get oxidised to –COOH: one is already –CHO (→COOH directly) and the other must be an alkyl group at the ortho position that oxidises to –COOH
Molecular formula C9H10O = C6H4(CHO)(C2H5): a benzaldehyde ring with CHO and an ortho ethyl group accounts for C6H4+CHO+C2H5 = C9H10O exactly, so the compound is 2-ethylbenzaldehyde

question: An organic compound (A) (molecular formula C8H16O2) was hydrolysed with dilute sulphuric acid to give a carboxylic acid (B) and an alcohol (C). Oxidation of (C) with chromic acid produced (B). (C) on dehydration gives but-1-ene. Write equations for the reactions involved.
solution:
(A) is butyl butanoate, CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH2CH2CH3. (B) is butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2COOH. (C) is butan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH.
Hydrolysis: CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH2CH2CH3 + H2O (dil. H2SO4) → CH3CH2CH2COOH (B) + CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (C).
Oxidation: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (C) + [O] (chromic acid) → CH3CH2CH2COOH (B).
Dehydration: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (C) → (conc. H2SO4, heat) → CH3CH2CH=CH2 (but-1-ene) + H2O.
steps: Since (C) dehydrates to but-1-ene (a terminal alkene), (C) must be a straight-chain primary alcohol with the same 4-carbon skeleton, i.e. butan-1-ol (dehydration of a primary alcohol typically favours the less-substituted/Hofmann-type alkene under these simple conditions, consistent with but-1-ene formation)
Since oxidation of (C) gives (B), and (C) is a primary alcohol, (B) must be the corresponding carboxylic acid: butanoic acid
Ester (A), C8H16O2, hydrolyses to acid (B, C4H8O2) + alcohol (C, C4H10O); C4+C4=C8 carbons check out, confirming (A) is butyl butanoate

question:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their property as indicated:
(i) Acetaldehyde, Acetone, Di-tert-butyl ketone, Methyl tert-butyl ketone (reactivity towards HCN)
(ii) CH3CH2CH(Br)COOH, CH3CH(Br)CH2COOH, (CH3)2CHCOOH, CH3CH2CH2COOH (acid strength)
(iii) Benzoic acid, 4-Nitrobenzoic acid, 3,4-Dinitrobenzoic acid, 4-Methoxybenzoic acid (acid strength)
solution:
(i) Di-tert-butyl ketone < Methyl tert-butyl ketone < Acetone < Acetaldehyde.
(ii) (CH3)2CHCOOH < CH3CH2CH2COOH < CH3CH(Br)CH2COOH < CH3CH2CH(Br)COOH.
(iii) 4-Methoxybenzoic acid < Benzoic acid < 4-Nitrobenzoic acid < 3,4-Dinitrobenzoic acid.
steps: (i) Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition (HCN) decreases with increasing steric bulk and increasing +I effect of alkyl substituents around the carbonyl carbon; aldehydes (least hindered, one H) are most reactive, and bulky di-tert-butyl ketone is least reactive

(ii) Acid strength increases with the inductive electron-withdrawing effect of the Br substituent, which is strongest when Br is closest to the –COOH group (α-position); isobutyric acid (no Br) is weakest, and 2-bromobutanoic acid (Br on the α-carbon) is strongest
(iii) Electron-withdrawing groups (–NO2) increase acid strength (more so with more nitro groups); electron-donating groups (–OCH3) decrease it relative to unsubstituted benzoic acid

question:
Give simple chemical tests to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds.
(i) Propanal and Propanone
(ii) Acetophenone and Benzophenone
(iii) Phenol and Benzoic acid
(iv) Benzoic acid and Ethyl benzoate
(v) Pentan-2-one and Pentan-3-one
(vi) Benzaldehyde and Acetophenone
(vii) Ethanal and Propanal
solution:
(i) Tollens' test: propanal (an aldehyde) gives a silver mirror; propanone (a ketone) does not.
(ii) Iodoform test: acetophenone (a methyl ketone, CH3CO-) gives a yellow iodoform precipitate with I2/NaOH; benzophenone (no CH3CO- group) does not.
(iii) FeCl3 test: phenol gives a violet/purple colouration with neutral FeCl3; benzoic acid does not (or gives at most a buff-coloured precipitate, not the characteristic violet colour) — alternatively, NaHCO3 test: benzoic acid liberates brisk CO2 effervescence with NaHCO3 (being a stronger, carboxylic acid), phenol (a much weaker acid) does not.
(iv) NaHCO3 test: benzoic acid liberates CO2 effervescence with aqueous NaHCO3; ethyl benzoate (an ester, not acidic) does not react.
(v) Iodoform test: pentan-2-one (CH3CO-CH2CH2CH3, a methyl ketone) gives a positive iodoform test (yellow precipitate); pentan-3-one (CH3CH2-CO-CH2CH3, not a methyl ketone) gives a negative iodoform test.
(vi) Tollens' test: benzaldehyde (an aldehyde) gives a silver mirror; acetophenone (a ketone) does not.
(vii) Iodoform test: ethanal (CH3CHO, a methyl-carbonyl-bearing aldehyde) gives a positive iodoform test; propanal (CH3CH2CHO, no CH3CO- group) gives a negative iodoform test.
steps: For aldehyde vs ketone: use Tollens' reagent (silver mirror test) — aldehydes give a positive result (silver mirror), ketones do not
For 'has a CH3CO– group' vs not: use the iodoform test (I2/NaOH) — a yellow precipitate of CHI3 indicates the methyl ketone/appropriate methyl carbinol pattern
For phenol vs carboxylic acid: use neutral FeCl3 (violet colour for phenol) or NaHCO3 (effervescence only for the stronger carboxylic acid)
For acid vs ester: NaHCO3 effervescence distinguishes the free carboxylic acid (reacts) from the ester (does not react)

question:
How will you prepare the following compounds from benzene? You may use any inorganic reagent and any organic reagent having not more than one carbon atom
(i) Methyl benzoate
(ii) m-Nitrobenzoic acid
(iii) p-Nitrobenzoic acid
(iv) Phenylacetic acid
(v) p-Nitrobenzaldehyde.
solution:
(i) Benzene → (CO + HCl, anhydrous AlCl3/CuCl, Gattermann-Koch reaction) → benzaldehyde → [O] (mild oxidant) → benzoic acid → (CH3OH/H2SO4, Fischer esterification) → methyl benzoate.
(ii) Benzene → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) → nitrobenzene → (KMnO4, vigorous oxidation... but nitrobenzene has no oxidisable side chain) — corrected route: benzene → (CO/HCl, AlCl3) → benzaldehyde → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4, meta-directing effect of CHO) → m-nitrobenzaldehyde → [O] → m-nitrobenzoic acid.
(iii) Benzene → (KMnO4 not applicable directly) — use: benzene → (COOH group installed first): benzene → (CO/HCl,AlCl3) benzaldehyde → [O] → benzoic acid (a meta-director) → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) → m-nitrobenzoic acid — this actually gives meta, not para; the standard NCERT route for para is: benzene → (CH3Cl/AlCl3, Friedel-Crafts) → toluene → (HNO3/H2SO4) → p-nitrotoluene (major, since CH3 is o,p-director) → [O] (KMnO4, vigorous, oxidises CH3 to COOH without touching NO2) → p-nitrobenzoic acid.
(iv) Benzene → (CH3Cl/AlCl3) → toluene → (Cl2/hv, benzylic) → benzyl chloride → (KCN, SN2) → phenylacetonitrile (C6H5CH2CN) → (H3O+, hydrolysis) → phenylacetic acid (C6H5CH2COOH).
(v) Benzene → (CH3Cl/AlCl3) → toluene → (HNO3/H2SO4) → p-nitrotoluene → (CrO3/Ac2O or CrO2Cl2, Etard reaction, controlled oxidation of the methyl to aldehyde) → p-nitrobenzaldehyde.
steps: (i) Build the one-carbon –CHO group via Gattermann-Koch (CO+HCl/AlCl3), oxidise mildly to the acid, then Fischer-esterify with methanol

(iii) Route via toluene (using CH3Cl, a permitted 1-carbon reagent, for Friedel-Crafts alkylation) exploits the o,p-directing methyl group for nitration, then vigorous KMnO4 oxidation of CH3→COOH (NO2 survives oxidation) to give the para product directly
(ii) For the meta-isomer, install the meta-directing group (CHO, via Gattermann-Koch) BEFORE nitration, so nitration occurs meta to it, then oxidise CHO to COOH
(iv) Chain-extend via toluene → benzylic chlorination → cyanide substitution (adds one carbon) → hydrolysis to the acid
(v) Reach p-nitrotoluene as in (iii)'s route, then use a controlled, milder oxidant (Etard reaction, CrO2Cl2) that stops at the aldehyde stage rather than going all the way to the acid

question:
How will you bring about the following conversions in not more than two steps?
(i) Propanone to Propene
(ii) Benzoic acid to Benzaldehyde
(iii) Ethanol to 3-Hydroxybutanal
(iv) Benzene to m-Nitroacetophenone
(v) Benzaldehyde to Benzophenone
(vi) Bromobenzene to 1-Phenylethanol
(vii) Benzaldehyde to 3-Phenylpropan-1-ol
(viii) Benazaldehyde to α-Hydroxyphenylacetic acid
(ix) Benzoic acid to m-Nitrobenzyl alcohol.
solution:
(i) Propanone → (NaBH4/LiAlH4, reduction) → propan-2-ol → (conc. H2SO4, dehydration) → propene.
(ii) Benzoic acid → (SOCl2) → benzoyl chloride → (H2/Pd-BaSO4, Rosenmund reduction) → benzaldehyde.
(iii) Ethanol → [O] (PCC) → ethanal → (dil. NaOH, aldol addition) → 3-hydroxybutanal.
(iv) Benzene → (CH3COCl/AlCl3, Friedel-Crafts acylation) → acetophenone → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4, meta-director –COCH3) → m-nitroacetophenone.
(v) Benzaldehyde → (C6H5MgBr, Grignard addition, then H3O+) → diphenylmethanol (benzhydrol) → [O] (mild oxidant, e.g. PCC) → benzophenone.
(vi) Bromobenzene → (Mg, dry ether) → phenylmagnesium bromide → (CH3CHO, then H3O+) → 1-phenylethanol.
(vii) Benzaldehyde → (CH3CHO/dil. NaOH, crossed aldol using acetaldehyde) → cinnamaldehyde (3-phenylprop-2-enal, C6H5CH=CHCHO) → (H2/Ni, reduces both C=C and C=O) → 3-phenylpropan-1-ol.
(viii) Benzaldehyde → (HCN, addition) → mandelonitrile (C6H5CH(OH)CN) → (H3O+, hydrolysis of nitrile to acid) → α-hydroxyphenylacetic acid (mandelic acid, C6H5CH(OH)COOH).
(ix) Benzoic acid → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) → m-nitrobenzoic acid → (LiAlH4, reduction of COOH to CH2OH) → m-nitrobenzyl alcohol.
steps: Each conversion uses at most two named standard reactions (reduction with NaBH4/LiAlH4/H2, dehydration, Rosenmund reduction, aldol addition/condensation, Friedel-Crafts acylation, directed nitration, Grignard addition, HCN addition + hydrolysis) to reach the target in the fewest steps
Pay attention to which reagent gives selective reduction (Rosenmund stops at the aldehyde; LiAlH4 reduces –COOH all the way to –CH2OH; NaBH4/PCC choose the appropriate oxidation level) at each stage

question:
Describe the following:
(i) Acetylation
(ii) Cannizzaro reaction
(iii) Cross aldol condensation
(iv) Decarboxylation
solution:
(i) Acetylation: introduction of an acetyl group (CH3CO–) into a molecule (typically replacing an active hydrogen of –OH or –NH2), usually using acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride, e.g. C6H5OH + (CH3CO)2O → C6H5OCOCH3 + CH3COOH (phenyl acetate).
(ii) Cannizzaro reaction: a base-catalysed (concentrated NaOH/KOH) disproportionation of an aldehyde having no α-hydrogen, in which one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate salt while another is simultaneously reduced to the corresponding alcohol, e.g. 2HCHO + NaOH → CH3OH + HCOONa.
(iii) Cross (mixed) aldol condensation: an aldol condensation between two different carbonyl compounds (at least one having α-hydrogens), giving a mixture of possible β-hydroxy/α,β-unsaturated products, e.g. condensation of an aromatic aldehyde (no α-H, e.g. benzaldehyde) with an aliphatic aldehyde/ketone having α-H gives predominantly one main product (via Claisen-Schmidt reaction), e.g. C6H5CHO + CH3COCH3 → (NaOH) → C6H5CH=CHCOCH3 (benzalacetone) + H2O.
(iv) Decarboxylation: the loss of CO2 from a carboxylic acid (or its salt), typically achieved by heating the sodium salt of the acid with soda lime (NaOH + CaO), giving a hydrocarbon with one fewer carbon, e.g. CH3COONa + NaOH → (CaO, Δ) → CH4 + Na2CO3.
steps: Acetylation = adding a CH3CO– group via acetic anhydride/acetyl chloride to active-hydrogen-bearing substrates
Cannizzaro = base-mediated self-redox disproportionation exclusive to non-enolisable aldehydes
Cross aldol condensation = aldol condensation between two DIFFERENT carbonyl partners, often used deliberately (Claisen-Schmidt) with one non-enolisable partner to control the product
Decarboxylation = removal of CO2 from a carboxylate salt (typically soda-lime/heat) to shorten the carbon chain by one carbon

question:
Give plausible explanation for each of the following:
(i) Cyclohexanone forms cyanohydrin in good yield but 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone does not.
(ii) There are two –NH2 groups in semicarbazide. However, only one is involved in the formation of semicarbazones.
(iii) During the preparation of esters from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst, the water or the ester should be removed as soon as it is formed.
solution:
(i) Nucleophilic addition of HCN to a ketone carbonyl requires the incoming CN⁻ nucleophile to approach the planar sp² carbonyl carbon, which then becomes tetrahedral (sp³); in 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone, the bulky methyl groups positioned on both carbons flanking the carbonyl (at C2 and C6) create severe steric hindrance around the carbonyl carbon, blocking the approach of the nucleophile and preventing (or greatly slowing) cyanohydrin formation, whereas unsubstituted cyclohexanone has no such steric blocking.
(ii) Semicarbazide, H2N–NH–CO–NH2, has two types of –NH2 group: one directly attached to the carbonyl carbon (a 'semi-amide'/urea-type nitrogen, whose lone pair is delocalised into the C=O by resonance, making it a poor nucleophile) and one attached to the adjacent NH (a hydrazine-type nitrogen, not conjugated with the carbonyl, and hence a much better/more nucleophilic amine). Only this second, more nucleophilic –NH2 (attached to –NH–) condenses with the carbonyl compound to form the semicarbazone, leaving the other, resonance-deactivated –NH2 (next to C=O) unreacted.
(iii) Esterification is a reversible, acid-catalysed equilibrium reaction (RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O). By Le Chatelier's principle, continuously removing one of the products (water, e.g. using a dehydrating agent or a Dean-Stark trap, or removing the volatile ester by distillation as it forms) shifts the equilibrium further to the right (towards more ester formation), increasing the overall yield of the ester.
steps: (i) Steric hindrance from bulky groups flanking the carbonyl carbon blocks nucleophilic addition, since the reaction requires the carbon to become tetrahedral
(ii) Only the non-conjugated (hydrazine-type) NH2 of semicarbazide is nucleophilic enough to attack the carbonyl carbon; the other NH2 is deactivated by resonance with the adjacent C=O
(iii) Esterification is a reversible equilibrium; removing a product (water or the ester itself) as it forms shifts the equilibrium towards products by Le Chatelier's principle, improving the yield

question: An organic compound contains 69.77% carbon, 11.63% hydrogen and rest oxygen. The molecular mass of the compound is 86. It does not reduce Tollens' reagent but forms an addition compound with sodium hydrogensulphite and give positive iodoform test. On vigorous oxidation it gives ethanoic and propanoic acid. Write the possible structure of the compound.
solution: The compound is pentan-2-one, CH3COCH2CH2CH3.
steps: Empirical formula from % composition: C: 69.77/12=5.81, H: 11.63/1=11.63, O: 18.60/16=1.16; dividing by smallest (1.16): C≈5, H≈10, O≈1, giving empirical formula C5H10O (mass=86, matching the given molecular mass, so molecular formula = C5H10O)
No reaction with Tollens' reagent ⇒ not an aldehyde ⇒ it is a ketone; addition with NaHSO3 confirms a carbonyl compound (aldehydes and methyl ketones both give this addition product)
Positive iodoform test ⇒ it is a methyl ketone (has a CH3CO– group)

Vigorous oxidative cleavage giving BOTH ethanoic acid (CH3COOH, 2 carbons) and propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH, 3 carbons) means the ketone, on cleavage at the C=O, gives a 2-carbon fragment (as acetic acid, from the CH3CO– end) and a 3-carbon fragment (as propanoic acid, from the other side, CH2CH2CH3 oxidised to COOH) — consistent with CH3-CO-CH2CH2CH3 (pentan-2-one), whose oxidative cleavage gives CH3COOH + CH3CH2COOH

question: Although phenoxide ion has more number of resonating structures than carboxylate ion, carboxylic acid is a stronger acid than phenol. Why?
solution: In the phenoxide ion, although there are several resonance structures, the negative charge is delocalised onto the ortho and para carbon atoms of the ring (i.e. onto carbon atoms, which are not very electronegative and do not stabilise negative charge as effectively), and some of these resonance structures also disrupt the aromaticity/are less stable (higher-energy contributors), so the overall stabilisation, while real, is comparatively modest. In the carboxylate ion, the negative charge is delocalised over just two structures, but both place the charge on the two (equivalent) highly electronegative oxygen atoms, which are much better able to stabilise negative charge; moreover, the two C–O bonds in carboxylate become exactly equivalent (each of intermediate, ~1.5, bond order), giving very effective and energetically favourable resonance stabilisation despite the smaller number of contributing structures. Since resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base (and hence acid strength) depends more on how effectively (not just how many times) the charge is delocalised — especially whether it resides on an electronegative atom — the carboxylate ion is considerably more stabilised than the phenoxide ion, making carboxylic acids significantly stronger acids than phenols.
steps: Compare where the delocalised negative charge actually resides: phenoxide spreads charge partly onto carbon atoms (less effective stabilisation, and some resonance structures are higher in energy/less favourable), while carboxylate spreads its charge equally over two equivalent, highly electronegative oxygen atoms
Effectiveness of resonance stabilisation (charge on electronegative atoms, equivalent low-energy structures) matters more than the raw count of resonance structures

Hence carboxylate's more effective (though numerically fewer) resonance stabilisation makes it the more stable conjugate base, so carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols despite phenoxide having more resonance forms

question:
Write IUPAC names of the following compounds and classify them into primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
(i) (CH3)2CHNH2
(ii) CH3(CH2)2NH2
(iii) CH3NHCH(CH3)2
(iv) (CH3)3CNH2
(v) C6H5NHCH3
(vi) (CH3CH2)2NCH3
(vii) m–BrC6H4NH2
solution:
(i) Propan-2-amine — primary.
(ii) Propan-1-amine — primary.
(iii) N-Methylpropan-2-amine — secondary.
(iv) 2-Methylpropan-2-amine — primary.
(v) N-Methylaniline (N-methylbenzenamine) — secondary.
(vi) N-Ethyl-N-methylethanamine — tertiary.
(vii) 3-Bromoaniline (3-Bromobenzenamine) — primary.
steps: Name the parent chain/ring bearing the –NH2/–NHR/–NR2 group, using 'amine' as suffix (or aniline for the aromatic parent) with N-substituent prefixes for any groups on the nitrogen
Classify by counting carbon groups directly bonded to N: one C group = primary, two = secondary, three = tertiary

question:
Give one chemical test to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds.
(i) Methylamine and dimethylamine
(ii) Secondary and tertiary amines
(iii) Ethylamine and aniline
(iv) Aniline and benzylamine
(v) Aniline and N-methylaniline.
solution:
(i) Carbylamine test (or Hinsberg test): methylamine (1°) with CHCl3/alc. KOH gives a foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine reaction, positive); dimethylamine (2°) gives no such reaction (negative).
(ii) Hinsberg's test: react with benzenesulphonyl chloride (C6H5SO2Cl) + KOH — a secondary amine gives an insoluble N,N-dialkylsulphonamide precipitate that does not dissolve in KOH; a tertiary amine does not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride (remains as an oily layer/unreacted, and simply dissolves in dilute acid).
(iii) Azo dye test (or carbylamine test): aniline (aromatic 1° amine) reacts with HNO2 at 273–278K to form a diazonium salt, which on coupling with an alkaline β-naphthol solution gives a bright orange-red azo dye; ethylamine (aliphatic 1° amine) reacts with HNO2 to evolve N2 gas with brisk effervescence, giving ethanol, and does not give an azo dye. (Alternatively, carbylamine test: both are 1° amines and both give a positive carbylamine test, so this specific test does NOT distinguish them — the azo dye/diazonium test is the correct distinguishing test.)
(iv) Azo dye test: aniline (aromatic amine, directly attached to ring) forms a diazonium salt at low temperature that couples with β-naphthol to give an orange-red azo dye; benzylamine (C6H5CH2NH2, an aliphatic primary amine since NH2 is on the CH2, not the ring) reacts with HNO2 to liberate N2 gas (no stable diazonium salt, no azo dye).
(v) Azo dye test: aniline (1° aromatic amine) with HNO2 (273-278K) forms a diazonium salt that gives an azo dye on coupling with β-naphthol/alkali; N-methylaniline (2° aromatic amine) with HNO2 instead forms a yellow oily N-nitroso compound (N-nitroso-N-methylaniline), not a diazonium salt, so no azo dye is formed.
steps: (i) Use the carbylamine reaction (positive foul smell only for 1° amines) to distinguish 1° from 2°
(ii) Use Hinsberg's test (benzenesulphonyl chloride) which gives distinctly different, characteristic solubility behaviour for 1°, 2° and 3° amines

(iii)-(v) Exploit the different reactivity of aliphatic vs aromatic (and 1° vs 2°) amines towards nitrous acid (HNO2): aliphatic 1° amines evolve N2 gas; aromatic 1° amines form a stable diazonium salt (tested via azo-dye coupling with β-naphthol); aromatic 2° amines form a yellow nitrosamine oil instead

question:
Account for the following:
(i) pKb of aniline is more than that of methylamine.
(ii) Ethylamine is soluble in water whereas aniline is not.
(iii) Methylamine in water reacts with ferric chloride to precipitate hydrated ferric oxide.
(iv) Although amino group is o– and p– directing in aromatic electrophilic substitution reactions, aniline on nitration gives a substantial amount of m-nitroaniline.
(v) Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(vi) Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.
(vii) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is preferred for synthesising primary amines.
solution:
(i) A higher pKb means a weaker base. Aniline is a much weaker base than methylamine because the lone pair on the aniline nitrogen is delocalised (by resonance) into the aromatic ring, making it far less available for protonation; also the sp² (partial) hybridisation of aniline's N and the electron-withdrawing inductive effect of the aromatic ring reduce electron density at N, whereas methylamine's nitrogen lone pair is fully available, and the +I effect of the methyl group further increases its basicity; hence aniline (weaker base, higher pKb) vs methylamine (stronger base, lower pKb).
(ii) Ethylamine, being a small molecule with an N–H capable of hydrogen bonding with water, is miscible with water; aniline has a large hydrophobic phenyl group that dominates its behaviour, making it only sparingly soluble in water despite having an N–H group, since the energetic cost of accommodating the bulky non-polar ring in water is not offset by the relatively weak N–H···O hydrogen bonding it can offer.
(iii) Methylamine is a weak base but is basic enough to react with water to generate OH⁻ ions (CH3NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3NH3⁺ + OH⁻); this OH⁻ then reacts with Fe³⁺ (from added FeCl3) to precipitate hydrated ferric oxide/hydroxide, Fe2O3·xH2O (or Fe(OH)3): FeCl3 + 3CH3NH2 + 3H2O → Fe(OH)3↓ + 3CH3NH3Cl.
(iv) Under the strongly acidic nitrating conditions (conc. HNO3/H2SO4), a significant fraction of the aniline is protonated to form the anilinium ion, C6H5NH3⁺; this positively-charged group is strongly electron-withdrawing (deactivating) and, unlike free –NH2, is a meta-director, so nitration of this protonated species occurs predominantly at the meta position, giving a substantial proportion of m-nitroaniline alongside the o/p products from the small amount of unprotonated aniline.
(v) In Friedel-Crafts reactions, the Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl3) forms a strong Lewis acid-base complex with the lone pair on the aniline nitrogen (–NH2 + AlCl3 → –NH2→AlCl3), which makes the nitrogen strongly electron-withdrawing (positively charged/complexed) instead of electron-donating; this deactivates the ring (now behaves like a meta-director/strongly deactivated ring) and prevents the Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation from proceeding normally.
(vi) Aromatic diazonium salts (ArN2⁺) are stabilised by resonance delocalisation of the positive charge into the aromatic ring (through conjugation of the ring π-system with the N≡N group), giving them extra stability even at low temperatures; aliphatic diazonium salts (RN2⁺) have no such ring to delocalise the charge into, so they are highly unstable and decompose immediately (even below 273K) to release N2 gas and form a carbocation.
(vii) The Gabriel phthalimide synthesis converts an alkyl halide (via the phthalimide anion, a good nucleophile, followed by hydrolysis) into a primary amine without any risk of over-alkylation, since the phthalimide nitrogen, after one substitution, no longer has an acidic N–H to lose and cannot react further with a second molecule of alkyl halide — unlike direct ammonolysis of alkyl halides (RX + NH3), which readily gives a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and even a quaternary ammonium salt due to further alkylation of the initially formed amine. Hence Gabriel synthesis gives clean, pure primary amines.
steps: (i) Resonance delocalisation of aniline's N lone pair into the ring reduces its availability for protonation, making it a much weaker base (higher pKb) than methylamine, whose lone pair is fully available and further enhanced by the +I methyl group
(ii) Aniline's large hydrophobic phenyl ring outweighs its limited H-bonding capacity via N-H, unlike the small, fully water-miscible ethylamine
(iii) Methylamine's weak basicity in water generates enough OH⁻ to precipitate Fe(OH)3/hydrated Fe2O3 from Fe³⁺
(iv) Under strongly acidic nitrating conditions, protonation converts some aniline into the meta-directing anilinium cation, giving significant meta product alongside the normal o/p products
(v) AlCl3 (Lewis acid catalyst) complexes with aniline's N lone pair, converting the ring-activating NH2 into a deactivating group, blocking Friedel-Crafts reaction
(vi) Aromatic diazonium ions are resonance-stabilised by the attached ring; aliphatic ones lack this stabilisation and decompose instantly
(vii) Gabriel synthesis avoids over-alkylation (no acidic N-H left after first substitution) unlike direct ammonolysis, giving clean primary amines

question:
Arrange the following:
(i) In decreasing order of the pKb values: C2H5NH2, C6H5NHCH3, (C2H5)2NH and C6H5NH2
(ii) In increasing order of basic strength: C6H5NH2, C6H5N(CH3)2, (C2H5)2NH and CH3NH2
(iii) In increasing order of basic strength: (a) Aniline, p-nitroaniline and p-toluidine (b) C6H5NH2, C6H5NHCH3, C6H5CH2NH2.
(iv) In decreasing order of basic strength in gas phase: C2H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, (C2H5)3N and NH3
(v) In increasing order of boiling point: C2H5OH, (CH3)2NH, C2H5NH2
(vi) In increasing order of solubility in water: C6H5NH2, (C2H5)2NH, C2H5NH2.
solution:
(i) C6H5NH2 < C6H5NHCH3 < C2H5NH2 < (C2H5)2NH (decreasing pKb means increasing basicity, so this lists from weakest base/highest pKb, aniline, to strongest base/lowest pKb, diethylamine).
(ii) C6H5NH2 < C6H5N(CH3)2 < CH3NH2 < (C2H5)2NH.
(iii) (a) p-nitroaniline < aniline < p-toluidine. (b) C6H5NH2 < C6H5NHCH3 < C6H5CH2NH2.
(iv) (C2H5)3N > (C2H5)2NH > C2H5NH2 > NH3.
(v) (CH3)2NH < C2H5NH2 < C2H5OH.
(vi) C6H5NH2 < (C2H5)2NH < C2H5NH2.
steps: (i)&(ii)&(iii) In aqueous solution, basicity of amines depends on a balance of +I effect (alkyl groups increase basicity), resonance/conjugation with an aromatic ring (decreases basicity by delocalising the lone pair), steric hindrance to solvation/protonation, and (for substituted anilines) the electronic effect of ring substituents (electron-withdrawing groups like NO2 decrease basicity further; electron-donating groups like CH3 increase it)

Aromatic amines (aniline, N-methylaniline) are weaker bases than aliphatic amines due to resonance delocalisation of the N lone pair into the ring; a benzylic amine (C6H5CH2NH2) is NOT conjugated with the ring (since NH2 is on the CH2, not directly on the ring) so it behaves essentially as an aliphatic amine (much more basic than aniline)

(iv) In the gas phase (no solvent effects), basicity increases purely with the number of electron-donating alkyl groups (+I effect, and no complicating steric/solvation factors), so tertiary > secondary > primary > NH3

(v) Boiling point correlates with hydrogen-bonding strength: alcohols (O–H) hydrogen-bond more strongly than primary amines (N–H, less polarised bond), and secondary amines have fewer N–H bonds available for hydrogen bonding than primary amines, so (CH3)2NH < C2H5NH2 < C2H5OH

(vi) Aqueous solubility depends on hydrogen-bonding ability balanced against hydrophobic bulk: aniline's large ring reduces solubility most; among the aliphatic amines, the secondary amine (fewer available N-H's relative to its larger hydrophobic bulk) is less soluble than the primary ethylamine

question:
How will you convert:
(i) Ethanoic acid into methanamine
(ii) Hexanenitrile into 1-aminopentane
(iii) Methanol to ethanoic acid
(iv) Ethanamine into methanamine
(v) Ethanoic acid into propanoic acid
(vi) Methanamine into ethanamine
(vii) Nitromethane into dimethylamine
(viii) Propanoic acid into ethanoic acid?
solution:
(i) CH3COOH → (NH3, heat, −H2O) → CH3CONH2 (acetamide) → (Br2/NaOH, Hofmann bromamide degradation, loses 1 carbon) → CH3NH2 (methanamine).
(ii) CH3(CH2)4CN → (H2/Ni or LiAlH4, reduction) → CH3(CH2)4CH2NH2 (1-aminohexane — note: to get 1-aminopentane specifically, i.e. one fewer carbon than the nitrile chain, use instead the Hofmann degradation route on the corresponding amide: hexanenitrile → partial hydrolysis → hexanamide → Br2/NaOH (Hofmann) → 1-aminopentane, losing the carbonyl carbon).
(iii) CH3OH → [O] (acidified KMnO4/K2Cr2O7) → HCHO → [O] → HCOOH — this gives methanoic acid, not ethanoic acid; to build ethanoic acid (one more carbon) from methanol: CH3OH → (PBr3/HBr) → CH3Br → (KCN) → CH3CN → (H3O+, hydrolysis) → CH3COOH (ethanoic acid).
(iv) CH3CH2NH2 → (HNO2, or via diazotisation then hydrolysis is not standard for aliphatic; standard route) CH3CH2NH2 has one carbon too many to reach CH3NH2 directly by a named reaction; practical route: degrade via the amide: CH3CH2NH2 is not simply shortened; standard textbook approach uses: CH3CH2COOH (from ethanamine via a multi-step oxidative route) is impractical — accepted simplest answer: ethanamine → (CHCl3/KOH, carbylamine, NOT a shortening reaction) — the standard accepted 2-step method is: convert ethanamine to ethanamide is not direct either. Given the complexity, the standard NCERT-accepted route is via degradation is omitted; a simpler accepted transformation uses: CH3CH2NH2 → (oxidise fully to CH3COOH via multi-step, then Hofmann degradation) CH3COOH → CH3CONH2 (NH3) → (Br2/NaOH) → CH3NH2.
(v) CH3COOH → (Cl2/red P, Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky) → ClCH2COOH → (KCN) → NCCH2COOH → (H3O+, hydrolysis, then decarboxylation is not needed since we just need chain to grow) — simpler accepted route: CH3COOH → (SOCl2) → CH3COCl → (with CH3MgBr is not selective) — standard accepted 2-step route: CH3COOH → (reduce to CH3CH2OH via LiAlH4) → CH3CH2OH → (PBr3) → CH3CH2Br → (KCN) → CH3CH2CN → (H3O+, hydrolysis) → CH3CH2COOH (propanoic acid).
(vi) CH3NH2 → (CHCl3/alc. KOH, carbylamine) → CH3NC (methyl isocyanide) → (H2/Ni or LiAlH4, reduction) → CH3CH2NH2 (ethanamine) — reduction of the isocyanide adds one carbon and converts N≡C to CH2NH2.
(vii) CH3NO2 → (Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl or H2/catalyst, reduction) → CH3NH2 (methanamine) → (CH3I, excess, exhaustive methylation) → (CH3)2NH (dimethylamine, controlling stoichiometry/isolating the secondary amine from the mixture).
(viii) CH3CH2COOH → (Cl2/red P, HVZ reaction) → CH3CHClCOOH → (aq. KOH/hydrolysis then further steps are for substitution, not shortening) — standard accepted shortening route uses the Hofmann bromamide type degradation via decarboxylation: CH3CH2COOH → (NH3) → CH3CH2CONH2 → (Br2/NaOH, Hofmann degradation) → CH3CH2NH2 (ethanamine, this shortens by removing carbonyl carbon) — to then get to ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) requires a different route entirely: propanoic acid → (soda lime decarboxylation is not selective) — simplest accepted method: propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, is treated with LiAlH4 to give propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH, then oxidative cleavage is not standard; instead the practical NCERT-style answer is via haloform-type degradation: propanoic acid → is often just accepted as requiring a 2-carbon-shortening oxidative decarboxylation (e.g. via the corresponding methyl ketone and iodoform reaction after appropriate functional group manipulation) — for the purposes of this answer, the essential concept tested is chain-shortening via amide formation and Hofmann degradation (which removes the carbonyl carbon), so propanoic acid → propanamide (NH3) → Hofmann degradation (Br2/NaOH) → ethanamine (CH3CH2NH2), and this ethanamine, on diazotisation/hydrolysis (NaNO2/HCl then H2O) is converted to ethanol, which is then oxidised (KMnO4) to ethanoic acid: CH3CH2NH2 → (NaNO2/HCl) → CH3CH2OH → [O] → CH3COOH.
steps: Chain-lengthening tool: convert -COOH/-OH to the halide, then displace with KCN to add one carbon as a nitrile, then hydrolyse (or reduce) the nitrile to the acid/amine as needed

Chain-shortening tool: convert the acid to its amide (with NH3) then apply the Hofmann bromamide degradation (Br2/NaOH), which removes the carbonyl carbon and gives an amine with one fewer carbon than the original acid

Amine-to-alcohol/acid tool: diazotise a primary aliphatic amine (NaNO2/HCl) to replace –NH2 with –OH (via an unstable diazonium ion that decomposes in water), then oxidise the resulting alcohol as needed

Nitroalkane-to-amine tool: simple catalytic/chemical reduction (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl or H2/catalyst) converts –NO2 to –NH2; further exhaustive alkylation (excess RX) converts a primary amine to secondary/tertiary/quaternary amines

Isocyanide-to-homologated-amine tool: reduction of an isocyanide (R–NC, itself made from R-NH2 + CHCl3/KOH) with H2/Ni or LiAlH4 gives the next-higher secondary... actually gives R-CH2-NH2, i.e. an amine with one more carbon than the original amine used to make the isocyanide

question: Describe a method for the identification of primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Also write chemical equations of the reactions involved.
solution:
Hinsberg's test is used: the amine is shaken with benzenesulphonyl chloride (C6H5SO2Cl) in the presence of aqueous KOH.
(1) A primary amine reacts to form an N-alkyl (or N-aryl) benzenesulphonamide with a replaceable/acidic N-H (since the remaining N–H is now flanked by the electron-withdrawing sulphonyl group, making it acidic): RNH2 + C6H5SO2Cl → C6H5SO2NHR + HCl. This sulphonamide is soluble in the excess aqueous KOH (as its potassium salt, since the acidic N-H is deprotonated), but a clear solution reprecipitates the free sulphonamide again upon acidification.
(2) A secondary amine reacts to form an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide with NO N–H remaining (both valences on N are alkyl groups plus the sulphonyl group): R2NH + C6H5SO2Cl → C6H5SO2NR2 + HCl. This product has no acidic hydrogen and is insoluble in aqueous KOH (remains as a precipitate/oily layer).
(3) A tertiary amine does not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride at all (no N–H available for substitution); it simply dissolves unreacted in the dilute acid used in the workup, and no precipitate/product forms with C6H5SO2Cl.
steps: Hinsberg's reagent (C6H5SO2Cl + KOH) reacts differently with 1°, 2° and 3° amines depending on how many N–H bonds remain available
1° amine → sulphonamide WITH one acidic N-H remaining → soluble in excess KOH (as its salt), reprecipitates on acidification
2° amine → sulphonamide with NO N-H remaining → insoluble in KOH
3° amine → no reaction at all with the sulphonyl chloride (no N-H to substitute) → remains unreacted, simply dissolves in dilute acid

question:
Write short notes on the following:
(i) Carbylamine reaction
(ii) Diazotisation
(iii) Hofmann's bromamide reaction
(iv) Coupling reaction
(v) Ammonolysis
(vi) Acetylation
(vii) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
solution:
(i) Carbylamine reaction: primary amines (aliphatic or aromatic), when heated with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, form isocyanides (carbylamines) with an offensive smell; this reaction is specific to primary amines and is used as a diagnostic test for them: RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH → RNC + 3KCl + 3H2O.
(ii) Diazotisation: the conversion of a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt by treating it with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO2 + HCl/dil. H2SO4) at a low temperature (273–278 K): C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl → (273-278K) → C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H2O.
(iii) Hofmann's bromamide reaction (degradation): a primary amide is converted into a primary amine having one carbon atom LESS than the original amide, by treating with bromine in the presence of aqueous or ethanolic NaOH/KOH: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → RNH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O.
(iv) Coupling reaction: an aromatic diazonium salt reacts with an activated aromatic compound (e.g. phenol or an amine) in weakly acidic/alkaline conditions to form a brightly coloured azo compound, containing the characteristic –N=N– (azo) linkage: C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ + C6H5OH → (NaOH) → C6H5N=N–C6H4OH-p + HCl.
(v) Ammonolysis: the nucleophilic substitution reaction in which an alkyl halide is treated with (usually excess/ethanolic) ammonia to replace the halogen with an amino group, forming a primary amine (though it often leads to further alkylation, giving a mixture of secondary, tertiary amines and a quaternary salt): RX + NH3 (excess, in a sealed tube, heated) → RNH2 + HX (the HX is absorbed as its ammonium salt, NH4X).
(vi) Acetylation: the introduction of an acetyl group (CH3CO–) into an amine (or alcohol/phenol) using acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride, converting an amine into an amide (acetamide derivative), which also moderates the amine's reactivity/basicity — useful, for example, before nitrating aniline to control over-oxidation/polysubstitution: C6H5NH2 + (CH3CO)2O → C6H5NHCOCH3 (acetanilide) + CH3COOH.
(vii) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: phthalimide is first converted to its potassium salt (using ethanolic KOH), which is then reacted with an alkyl halide (SN2) to give N-alkylphthalimide; this is subsequently hydrolysed (with aqueous NaOH or acid) to release a pure primary amine and phthalic acid/its salt — this method is specific to primary amines and cannot be used to prepare aromatic primary amines (since aryl halides do not undergo the required SN2 substitution).
steps: Each is a standard named reaction/process in amine chemistry: carbylamine (test for 1° amines), diazotisation (ArNH2→ArN2⁺ at low T), Hofmann bromamide degradation (amide→amine, one carbon shorter), azo coupling (ArN2⁺ + activated arene → azo dye), ammonolysis (RX+NH3→amine, often over-alkylates), acetylation (amine→amide, moderates reactivity), and Gabriel synthesis (clean route to pure 1° amines, aliphatic only)
State the defining reagents/conditions and a representative equation for each

question:
Accomplish the following conversions:
(i) Nitrobenzene to benzoic acid
(ii) Benzene to m-bromophenol
(iii) Benzoic acid to aniline
(iv) Aniline to 2,4,6-tribromofluorobenzene
(v) Benzyl chloride to 2-phenylethanamine
(vi) Chlorobenzene to p-chloroaniline
(vii) Aniline to p-bromoaniline
(viii) Benzamide to toluene
(ix) Aniline to benzyl alcohol.
solution:
(i) Nitrobenzene → (Sn/HCl, reduction) → aniline → (NaNO2/HCl, 273-278K, diazotisation) → benzenediazonium chloride → (CuCN, Sandmeyer) → benzonitrile → (H3O+, hydrolysis) → benzoic acid.
(ii) Benzene → (Br2/FeBr3) → bromobenzene → (conc. H2SO4, sulphonation) → p-bromobenzenesulphonic acid (protects the para position) → (conc. HNO3, nitration at the position ortho/meta as needed is complex) — simplified standard route: benzene → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) → nitrobenzene → (Br2/Fe, meta-directed by NO2) → m-bromonitrobenzene → (Sn/HCl, reduction) → m-bromoaniline → (NaNO2/HCl, then H3O+/heat, diazotisation and hydrolysis) → m-bromophenol.
(iii) Benzoic acid → (NH3, heat) → ammonium benzoate → (further heat, −H2O) → benzamide → (Br2/NaOH, Hofmann degradation) → aniline.
(iv) Aniline → (Br2 water, excess) → 2,4,6-tribromoaniline → (NaNO2/HCl, 273-278K) → 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride → (HBF4, then heat, Balz-Schiemann reaction) → 2,4,6-tribromofluorobenzene.
(v) Benzyl chloride → (KCN) → phenylacetonitrile (C6H5CH2CN) → (H2/Ni or LiAlH4, reduction) → 2-phenylethanamine (C6H5CH2CH2NH2).
(vi) Chlorobenzene → (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) → p-nitrochlorobenzene (major, o,p-director Cl) → (Sn/HCl, reduction of NO2, Cl survives) → p-chloroaniline.
(vii) Aniline → (protect first: (CH3CO)2O, acetylation) → acetanilide → (Br2/CH3COOH or Br2/water, mild bromination, now o,p-directed by NHCOCH3, mainly para due to steric bulk) → p-bromoacetanilide → (hydrolysis, aq. HCl/NaOH) → p-bromoaniline.
(viii) Benzamide → (Br2/NaOH, Hofmann degradation) → aniline → (NaNO2/HCl, 273-278K) → benzenediazonium chloride → (H3PO2/H2O, or ethanol, reduction/deamination) → benzene → (CH3Cl/AlCl3, Friedel-Crafts alkylation) → toluene.
(ix) Aniline → (NaNO2/HCl, 273-278K, diazotisation) → benzenediazonium chloride → (CuCN, Sandmeyer) → benzonitrile → (DIBAL-H, or SnCl2/HCl then hydrolysis, partial reduction to aldehyde) → benzaldehyde → (NaBH4, reduction) → benzyl alcohol.
steps: Chain each conversion through standard named steps: reduction (nitro→amine), diazotisation (aromatic amine→diazonium salt at 273-278K), and diazonium substitution reactions (Sandmeyer for CN/halogens, Balz-Schiemann for F, H3PO2 for deamination/H replacement, hydrolysis for OH)

Use protecting-group strategy (acetylation of aniline before halogenation) where needed to moderate the powerful activating effect of –NH2 and control substitution position/avoid oxidation side-reactions
Use CN⁻ substitution + reduction to homologate a benzylic halide by one carbon into an amine (v), and partial nitrile reduction (DIBAL-H) to stop cleanly at the aldehyde stage (ix)

question:
Give the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions:
(i) CH3CH2I → (NaCN) A → (H2/Ni) B → (NaNO2/HCl, then partial hydrolysis) C
(ii) C6H5NH2 → (NaNO2/HCl, 273K) A → (CuCN) B → (H3O+) C
(iii) CH3CH2Br → (KCN) A → (LiAlH4) B → (HNO2, 273K) C
(iv) C6H5NO2 → (Fe/HCl) A → (NaNO2/HCl, 273K) B → (H3O+/H2O) C
(v) CH3COOH → (NH3) A → (Br2/NaOH) B → (NaNO2/HCl then NaOBr) C
(vi) C6H5NO2 → (Fe/HCl) A → (HNO2, 273K) B → (C6H5OH) C
solution:
(i) A = CH3CH2CN (propanenitrile); B = CH3CH2CH2NH2 (1-aminopropane/propan-1-amine); C = CH3CH2CH2OH (propan-1-ol, via diazotisation and hydrolysis of the amine).
(ii) A = C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ (benzenediazonium chloride); B = C6H5CN (benzonitrile, via Sandmeyer reaction); C = C6H5COOH (benzoic acid, via hydrolysis of the nitrile).
(iii) A = CH3CH2CN (propanenitrile); B = CH3CH2CH2NH2 (propan-1-amine, via LiAlH4 reduction of the nitrile); C = CH3CH2CH2OH (propan-1-ol, via diazotisation/hydrolysis).
(iv) A = C6H5NH2 (aniline); B = C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ (benzenediazonium chloride); C = C6H5OH (phenol, via hydrolysis of the diazonium salt).
(v) A = CH3CONH2 (acetamide); B = CH3NH2 (methanamine, via Hofmann degradation); C = CH3NHBr → further reaction with NaOBr on the resulting amine can give N-bromination, but the standard intended sequence here treats CH3NH2 with NaOBr as an alternative synthesis pathway analogous to Hofmann's reagent itself; taking the question's intent (parallel to (ii)/(iv)) C is best identified as methanol, CH3OH (via diazotisation of B with NaNO2/HCl, then hydrolysis) — note NaOBr is essentially Hofmann's own brominating base, so this sub-question mirrors the standard degradation sequence, and C = CH3NH2 (i.e. B) is the final identifiable product of the classic sequence acid→amide→amine.
(vi) A = C6H5NH2 (aniline); B = C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ (benzenediazonium chloride, via diazotisation); C = C6H5N=N-C6H4OH-p (an azo dye, 4-hydroxyazobenzene, via coupling of the diazonium salt with phenol).
steps: Track each named reaction's standard product: NaCN/KCN on an alkyl halide gives a nitrile (adds 1 carbon); H2/Ni or LiAlH4 reduces a nitrile to a primary amine; NaNO2/HCl at 273K diazotises an aromatic primary amine (or decomposes an aliphatic one, eventually to the alcohol after hydrolysis); CuCN on a diazonium salt gives a nitrile (Sandmeyer); H3O+ hydrolyses a nitrile to a carboxylic acid; Fe/HCl reduces nitro to amine; coupling of a diazonium salt with phenol gives an azo dye
Apply the relevant sequence of these standard transformations to each starting material to identify A, B, C at each step

question: An aromatic compound 'A' on treatment with aqueous ammonia and heating forms compound 'B' which on heating with Br2 and KOH forms a compound 'C' of molecular formula C6H7N. Write the structures and IUPAC names of compounds A, B and C.
solution: A is benzoic acid, C6H5COOH. B is benzamide, C6H5CONH2 (benzenecarboxamide). C is aniline, C6H5NH2 (benzenamine), molecular formula C6H7N.
steps: A reacting with aqueous ammonia and heat to give an amide (B) indicates A is a carboxylic acid (or its derivative); the simplest aromatic acid is benzoic acid

B (an amide) on Hofmann bromamide degradation (Br2/KOH) gives a primary amine with one fewer carbon than the amide — from benzamide (C6H5CONH2, 7 carbons) this gives aniline (C6H5NH2, 6 carbons), matching the given molecular formula C6H7N
Hence A = benzoic acid, B = benzamide, C = aniline

question:
Complete the following reactions:
(i) C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + alc.KOH →
(ii) C6H5N2Cl + H3PO2 + H2O →
(iii) C6H5NH2 + conc. H2SO4 →
(iv) C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH →
(v) C2H5NH2 + Br2(aq) →
(vi) C6H5NH2 + (CH3CO)2O →
(vii) C6H5N2Cl → (i) HBF4 (ii) NaNO2/Cu →
solution:
(i) C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH(alc.) → C6H5NC (phenyl isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H2O (carbylamine reaction).
(ii) C6H5N2Cl + H3PO2 + H2O → C6H6 (benzene) + N2 + H3PO3 + HCl (reductive deamination of the diazonium salt).
(iii) C6H5NH2 + conc. H2SO4 → (heat, ~453K) C6H4(NH2)(SO3H)-p, i.e. sulphanilic acid (4-aminobenzenesulphonic acid, existing as a zwitterion) + H2O.
(iv) C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH → C6H6 (benzene) + N2 + CH3CHO + HCl (ethanol acts as a reducing agent, itself oxidised to acetaldehyde).
(v) C2H5NH2 + Br2(aq) → this does not give the classic aromatic-type bromination; for a primary aliphatic amine, excess Br2 with base can lead to N-bromination or oxidative side reactions, but under simple aqueous bromine water conditions, ethylamine is too reactive/basic and mainly just forms the ammonium salt/addition complex; the more standard NCERT-intended analogous reaction for this reagent combination applies to aniline (giving 2,4,6-tribromoaniline) rather than ethylamine — treating this literally, aqueous Br2 with excess ethylamine typically causes simple acid-base/complexation rather than a clean substitution product.
(vi) C6H5NH2 + (CH3CO)2O → C6H5NHCOCH3 (acetanilide) + CH3COOH.
(vii) C6H5N2Cl + HBF4 → C6H5N2BF4 (benzenediazonium fluoroborate) → (heat/dry, decomposition) → C6H5F (fluorobenzene) + N2 + BF3 (Balz-Schiemann reaction). Separately, C6H5N2Cl + NaNO2/Cu (Sandmeyer-type with Cu catalyst) → C6H5NO2 (nitrobenzene), replacing the diazonium group with –NO2.
steps: Apply the standard named reaction associated with each specific reagent combination on the amine/diazonium salt substrate: CHCl3/KOH→carbylamine; H3PO2/H2O→reductive deamination (removes N2, replaces with H); conc. H2SO4/heat on aniline→sulphanilic acid formation; C2H5OH on a diazonium salt→reductive deamination (ethanol as reductant, itself oxidised to acetaldehyde); (CH3CO)2O→acetylation; HBF4 then heat on diazonium→Balz-Schiemann (gives ArF); NaNO2/Cu on diazonium→replaces N2⁺ with NO2 (Sandmeyer-type)

question: Why cannot aromatic primary amines be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?
solution: The Gabriel phthalimide synthesis requires an SN2 nucleophilic substitution step, in which the phthalimide anion (nucleophile) attacks the electrophilic carbon of an alkyl halide, displacing the halide. Aryl halides (like bromobenzene, chlorobenzene) do not undergo this SN2 substitution under the reaction conditions, because the aromatic C–X bond has partial double-bond character (from resonance with the ring) and the sp² carbon is not accessible to backside nucleophilic attack; there is essentially no reaction between aryl halides and the phthalimide anion. Since aryl halides cannot be used as the electrophilic substrate in this synthesis, aromatic primary amines (which would require an aryl halide starting material) cannot be prepared by this method.
steps: Gabriel synthesis relies on SN2 displacement of a halide from an alkyl halide by the phthalimide anion
Aryl (and vinyl) halides do not undergo SN2 substitution (their C-X bond is not attackable from the backside; it has partial double-bond character from ring resonance)
So this method can only work with alkyl (aliphatic) halides, and cannot be extended to make aromatic (aryl) primary amines

question: Write the reactions of (i) aromatic and (ii) aliphatic primary amines with nitrous acid.
solution:
(i) Aromatic primary amines react with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO2 + HCl) at low temperature (273–278 K) to form a stable aromatic diazonium salt: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl → (273-278K) → C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H2O.
(ii) Aliphatic primary amines react with nitrous acid to form an unstable aliphatic diazonium salt, which is not stable even at low temperature and decomposes immediately, releasing nitrogen gas (with brisk effervescence) and forming a primary alcohol (via a carbocation intermediate, with the alcohol formed as the major product along with minor amounts of alkene/alkyl halide byproducts): CH3CH2NH2 + HNO2 → CH3CH2OH + N2↑ + H2O.
steps: (i) Aromatic amines give a STABLE diazonium salt at low T because the ring stabilises the positive charge by resonance
(ii) Aliphatic amines give an UNSTABLE diazonium salt that decomposes at once (even at 273K) with loss of N2 gas, yielding mainly the corresponding alcohol

question:
Give plausible explanation for each of the following:
(i) Why are amines less acidic than alcohols of comparable molecular masses?
(ii) Why do primary amines have higher boiling point than tertiary amines?
(iii) Why are aliphatic amines stronger bases than aromatic amines?
solution:
(i) Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so the N–H bond in amines is less polarised than the O–H bond in alcohols, meaning the hydrogen in amines is held more tightly/less readily released as H⁺; also, the conjugate base formed by deprotonating an amine (an amide ion, R-NH⁻) is much less stable (nitrogen is less able to stabilise the resulting negative charge than the more electronegative oxygen in an alkoxide ion, RO⁻), so amines are considerably less acidic than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.
(ii) Primary amines (R–NH2) have two N–H bonds available for intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas tertiary amines (R3N) have no N–H bonds at all (nitrogen's lone pair has no hydrogen to donate for hydrogen bonding, only weaker dipole-dipole/van der Waals forces are possible); since hydrogen bonding is stronger than these other forces, primary amines require more energy to vaporise, giving them a higher boiling point than tertiary amines of comparable molecular mass (secondary amines, with one N-H, are intermediate).
(iii) In aliphatic amines, the nitrogen lone pair is fully localised and available for donation to a proton (basicity), and is further made more available by the electron-donating (+I) effect of the attached alkyl group(s). In aromatic amines (e.g. aniline), the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised by resonance/conjugation into the aromatic π-system, making it much less available for protonation; additionally, the ring is electron-withdrawing by induction (sp² carbon), further reducing the electron density on nitrogen. Hence aliphatic amines, with their fully localised and enhanced lone pair, are stronger bases than aromatic amines, whose lone pair is substantially delocalised and less available.
steps: (i) Lower electronegativity of N (vs O) gives a less polar/less easily ionised N-H bond, and the resulting amide-ion conjugate base is less stabilised than an alkoxide, making amines weaker acids than alcohols
(ii) More N-H bonds (as in 1° amines) allow more/stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonding than fewer or no N-H bonds (as in 3° amines), raising the boiling point of the more H-bonded species

(iii) The aromatic ring's resonance delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair (into the ring π-system) makes it far less available for protonation compared to the fully localised, alkyl-enhanced lone pair of an aliphatic amine, making aromatic amines weaker bases

question: What are monosaccharides?
solution: Monosaccharides (also called simple sugars) are carbohydrates that cannot be hydrolysed further into simpler polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone units. They are the simplest carbohydrates and serve as the basic building blocks of oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Examples include glucose (an aldohexose), fructose (a ketohexose) and ribose (an aldopentose).
steps: Monosaccharides = simplest carbohydrate units, not further hydrolysable into simpler sugars
They are generally polyhydroxy aldehydes (aldoses, e.g. glucose) or polyhydroxy ketones (ketoses, e.g. fructose)
Examples: glucose, fructose, ribose, galactose

question: What are reducing sugars?
solution: Reducing sugars are carbohydrates that can reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent (i.e. their free aldehyde or ketone group, or a group that can be converted into one via the open-chain tautomer, is available to act as a reducing agent). All monosaccharides (both aldoses and ketoses) are reducing sugars, and among disaccharides, those with a free anomeric (hemiacetal) –OH group (e.g. maltose, lactose) are reducing sugars, whereas disaccharides in which both anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic linkage (e.g. sucrose) are non-reducing sugars.
steps: Reducing sugars reduce Tollens'/Fehling's reagent because they possess a free (or freely convertible via ring-chain tautomerism) aldehyde/ketone (hemiacetal) group
All monosaccharides are reducing sugars
Disaccharides are reducing only if at least one anomeric carbon is free (not used in the glycosidic bond), e.g. maltose and lactose are reducing, sucrose is non-reducing

question: Write two main functions of carbohydrates in plants.
solution: (1) Carbohydrates (in the form of starch) act as the storage form of energy in plants — plants store excess glucose produced by photosynthesis as starch in seeds, tubers and roots for later use as an energy reserve. (2) Carbohydrates (in the form of cellulose) provide structural support — cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, giving rigidity and mechanical strength to the plant.
steps: Function 1: energy storage — starch stores glucose/energy reserves in plants
Function 2: structural role — cellulose provides the structural framework of plant cell walls

question:
Classify the following into monosaccharides and disaccharides.
Ribose, 2-deoxyribose, maltose, galactose, fructose and lactose.
solution:
Monosaccharides: Ribose, 2-deoxyribose, galactose, fructose.
Disaccharides: Maltose, lactose.
steps: Monosaccharides are single sugar units that cannot be hydrolysed further: ribose (aldopentose), 2-deoxyribose (aldopentose), galactose (aldohexose), fructose (ketohexose)
Disaccharides are made of two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic linkage, hydrolysable into two monosaccharides: maltose (glucose+glucose) and lactose (glucose+galactose)

question: What do you understand by the term glycosidic linkage?
solution: A glycosidic linkage is the oxygen-bridge covalent bond (an acetal-type linkage) formed between the anomeric carbon (C1, the hemiacetal carbon) of one monosaccharide unit and a hydroxyl group of another monosaccharide (or other molecule), with loss of a water molecule. This linkage joins two monosaccharide units together to form a disaccharide (and repeated glycosidic linkages join many monosaccharide units to form oligosaccharides and polysaccharides).
steps: Glycosidic linkage = an acetal-type C–O–C bond formed between the anomeric (C1) carbon of one sugar and an –OH group of another sugar molecule, with elimination of water
It is the bond that links monosaccharide units together in disaccharides and polysaccharides

question: What is glycogen? How is it different from starch?
solution: Glycogen is the storage form of carbohydrate (a branched polymer of α-D-glucose units) found in animals, stored mainly in the liver and muscles — it is often called 'animal starch'. It differs from starch in that: (1) Glycogen is found in animal tissues (liver, muscle), whereas starch is found in plants (seeds, tubers). (2) Glycogen has a much more highly branched structure than amylopectin (the branched component of starch), with branching occurring more frequently. (3) Glycogen is readily and rapidly mobilised (broken down) to release glucose for quick energy needs in the body, being metabolically more active than starch.
steps: Glycogen = 'animal starch', a highly branched α-D-glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle of animals, used for quick-release energy
Difference from starch: source (animal vs plant), degree of branching (glycogen is more highly branched than even amylopectin), and metabolic role (glycogen is rapidly mobilised for quick energy)

question:
What are the hydrolysis products of
(i) sucrose and
(ii) lactose?
solution:
(i) Sucrose on hydrolysis gives one molecule of α-D-glucose and one molecule of β-D-fructose (this equimolar mixture is called invert sugar).
(ii) Lactose on hydrolysis gives one molecule of β-D-galactose and one molecule of β-D-glucose.
steps: (i) Sucrose = glucose + fructose joined via their anomeric carbons (a non-reducing disaccharide); hydrolysis (acid or the enzyme invertase/sucrase) cleaves this bond to give free glucose + fructose
(ii) Lactose = galactose + glucose linked via a glycosidic bond; hydrolysis (acid or the enzyme lactase) gives free galactose + glucose

question: What is the basic structural difference between starch and cellulose?
solution: Both starch (specifically its amylose component) and cellulose are polymers of glucose, but they differ in the type of glycosidic linkage joining the glucose units: starch (amylose) consists of glucose units joined by α-1,4-glycosidic linkages (giving a helical, coiled structure that is digestible by humans), whereas cellulose consists of glucose units joined by β-1,4-glycosidic linkages (giving long, straight, unbranched chains that pack together via extensive hydrogen bonding into rigid fibres, and which humans cannot digest since we lack the enzyme cellulase to hydrolyse β-linkages).
steps: Both are glucose polymers, but differ in the anomeric configuration of the glycosidic bond: starch (amylose) uses α-1,4-glycosidic linkages; cellulose uses β-1,4-glycosidic linkages
This structural difference gives starch a helical, digestible structure, while cellulose forms straight, rigid, hydrogen-bonded fibrous chains that are not digestible by humans

question:
What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents?
(i) HI
(ii) Bromine water
(iii) HNO3
solution:
(i) Prolonged/strong reduction of D-glucose with HI (concentrated, and heat) reduces all the –OH groups and the carbonyl completely, giving n-hexane, showing that all 6 carbon atoms of glucose are linked in a straight (unbranched) chain: CH3(CH2)4CH3.
(ii) Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent that selectively oxidises the aldehyde group (–CHO) of glucose to a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) without affecting the –OH groups, giving gluconic acid: CH2OH(CHOH)4COOH.
(iii) Dilute (or moderately concentrated) HNO3 is a stronger oxidising agent that oxidises BOTH the terminal –CHO group AND the terminal primary –CH2OH group of glucose to –COOH groups, giving a dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid (glucaric acid): COOH(CHOH)4COOH.
steps: (i) Exhaustive reduction (HI, red P, strong conditions) removes all oxygen functionality, revealing the underlying straight 6-carbon skeleton as n-hexane — evidence for glucose's linear carbon chain
(ii) Br2 water is a mild, chemoselective oxidant that only oxidises the aldehyde (–CHO→–COOH), giving the monocarboxylic gluconic acid
(iii) Dilute HNO3 is stronger and oxidises both the aldehyde AND the terminal primary alcohol to –COOH groups, giving the dicarboxylic saccharic (glucaric) acid

question: Enumerate the reactions of D-glucose which cannot be explained by its open chain structure.
solution: (1) Glucose does not give the Schiff's test (does not restore the colour of Schiff's reagent), even though it possesses a free –CHO group according to its open-chain structure — this suggests the aldehyde group is not freely available in the predominant form of glucose. (2) Glucose forms a pentaacetate (reacting with only 5, not the expected 6, acetyl groups on treatment with acetic anhydride), whereas the open-chain structure with 5 –OH groups plus one –CHO group would be expected to give a hexaacetate if the CHO also reacted (or more precisely, the open-chain form's 5 OH's would give a pentaacetate but the observed inertness of the carbonyl to certain tests still needs explanation). (3) Despite having a free aldehyde group in the open-chain form, glucose does not undergo some of the characteristic aldehyde reactions (like the 2,4-DNP test / bisulphite addition test giving a crystalline, non-glucose-typical product in the expected simple manner), and D-glucose exists in two different crystalline forms (α and β) with different physical properties (like specific rotation) despite being drawn as having identical open-chain structures — this phenomenon (mutarotation, and the existence of two anomers) cannot be explained by a simple open-chain structure. These observations are explained instead by glucose existing predominantly in a cyclic (pyranose, six-membered ring hemiacetal) form, in which the aldehyde carbon (C1) becomes a new stereocentre (the anomeric carbon) bonded to an –OH group, accounting for the two anomers (α and β), their interconversion (mutarotation), and the reduced typical aldehyde reactivity.
steps: Glucose fails to give a positive Schiff's test, unlike a 'normal' free aldehyde, despite its open-chain structure implying a free -CHO
Glucose forms a pentaacetate (not a hexaacetate), and its aldehyde-related reactivity is muted/altered compared to what the open-chain structure alone would predict

Glucose exists as two distinct crystalline anomers (α and β) with different specific rotations that interconvert in solution (mutarotation) — a phenomenon the open-chain structure alone cannot explain, but which is explained by cyclisation of the open-chain form into a six-membered (pyranose) hemiacetal ring, creating a new anomeric stereocentre at C1

question: What are essential and non-essential amino acids? Give two examples of each type.
solution: Essential amino acids are those that the human (or animal) body cannot synthesise on its own (or cannot synthesise in adequate amounts) and must therefore be obtained through the diet. Examples: valine, leucine (also isoleucine, lysine, threonine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan). Non-essential amino acids are those that the body can synthesise itself (in adequate quantities) from other metabolic precursors, so they need not necessarily be supplied through diet. Examples: glycine, alanine (also serine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, proline).
steps: Essential amino acids: cannot be synthesised by the body, must come from diet — e.g. valine, leucine
Non-essential amino acids: can be synthesised by the body itself — e.g. glycine, alanine

question:
Define the following as related to proteins
(i) Peptide linkage
(ii) Primary structure
(iii) Denaturation.
solution:
(i) Peptide linkage: the amide bond (–CO–NH–) formed between the –COOH group of one amino acid and the –NH2 group of the next amino acid, with elimination of a water molecule; it is the linkage that joins amino acids together to form peptides and proteins.
(ii) Primary structure: the specific, unique linear sequence in which the various amino acids are arranged (linked by peptide bonds) in a protein/polypeptide chain — even a single change in this sequence can alter the protein's identity and biological function.
(iii) Denaturation: the process by which a protein loses its native, biologically active three-dimensional structure (secondary and tertiary structure, i.e. its specific folding) due to a physical change (e.g. heat, UV light) or a chemical change (e.g. change in pH, addition of certain reagents), causing it to lose its characteristic biological activity, while the primary structure (sequence of amino acids/peptide bonds) generally remains unaffected.
steps: (i) Peptide linkage = the –CO–NH– amide bond formed between adjacent amino acids' -COOH and -NH2 groups, releasing water
(ii) Primary structure = the specific linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain

(iii) Denaturation = loss of a protein's native 3D folded structure (and hence biological activity) due to physical/chemical disturbance, while the amino acid sequence (primary structure) itself is unaffected

question: What are the common types of secondary structure of proteins?
solution: The two common types of secondary structure of proteins are: (1) the α-helix, a right-handed spiral/coiled structure in which the polypeptide backbone twists around an imaginary axis, stabilised by intramolecular hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one amino acid and the N–H of another amino acid four residues further along the same chain; and (2) the β-pleated sheet, in which two or more extended polypeptide chains (or segments of the same chain) lie side by side and are held together by intermolecular (or interstrand) hydrogen bonds, giving a folded, sheet-like/pleated arrangement.
steps: α-helix: a spiral coil stabilised by regular intramolecular (within a single chain) hydrogen bonding between backbone C=O and N-H groups
β-pleated sheet: extended polypeptide strands arranged side by side, held together by intermolecular/interstrand hydrogen bonds, giving a pleated sheet-like structure

question: What type of bonding helps in stabilising the α-helix structure of proteins?
solution: The α-helix structure is stabilised by intramolecular hydrogen bonds, specifically formed between the carbonyl oxygen (C=O) of one amino acid residue's peptide bond and the amide hydrogen (N–H) of another amino acid residue that is four positions further along the same polypeptide chain — these regularly repeating hydrogen bonds run roughly parallel to the helix axis and hold the coiled structure in place.
steps: The α-helix is held together entirely by intramolecular hydrogen bonding (within the same polypeptide chain), specifically between each residue's C=O and the N–H of the residue four units ahead in the chain, repeated regularly along the whole helix

question: Differentiate between globular and fibrous proteins.
solution: Fibrous proteins consist of long, thread-like polypeptide chains lying parallel/coiled around one another, held together by strong hydrogen bonds and (sometimes) disulphide bonds, forming fibre-like bundles; they are generally insoluble in water, and are typically structural proteins providing mechanical strength (e.g. keratin in hair/nails, myosin in muscle, collagen in tendons). Globular proteins consist of polypeptide chains that fold up compactly into a spherical/globular shape, with the hydrophobic groups usually turned inward and the hydrophilic groups on the surface; they are generally soluble in water, and typically perform dynamic biological functions (e.g. insulin, enzymes such as pepsin, and other regulatory/transport proteins).
steps: Fibrous proteins: long, thread-like, parallel chains held by H-bonds/disulphide bonds, insoluble in water, structural roles (keratin, myosin, collagen)
Globular proteins: compactly folded, spherical shape, generally water-soluble, dynamic/functional roles (insulin, enzymes)

question: How do you explain the amphoteric behaviour of amino acids?
solution: Amino acids contain both a basic group (the –NH2 amino group) and an acidic group (the –COOH carboxylic acid group) on the same molecule. In aqueous solution, an internal acid-base (proton transfer) reaction occurs: the carboxylic acid group donates a proton to the amino group, giving a dipolar/zwitterionic species (with a negatively charged –COO⁻ and a positively charged –NH3⁺ on the same molecule). Because of this zwitterionic form, amino acids can react as an acid (donating a proton from –NH3⁺, in basic medium) or as a base (accepting a proton at –COO⁻, in acidic medium) depending on the pH of the surrounding medium — this dual acid/base reactivity is what is meant by their amphoteric behaviour.
steps: Amino acids have both an acidic (-COOH) and a basic (-NH2) group in the same molecule, which react intramolecularly to form a zwitterion (-COO⁻ and -NH3⁺)
This zwitterion can act as an acid (donating H⁺ from -NH3⁺ in alkaline medium) or as a base (accepting H⁺ at -COO⁻ in acidic medium), giving amino acids their characteristic amphoteric behaviour

question: What are enzymes?
solution: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost all of which are globular proteins, that catalyse (speed up) specific biochemical reactions occurring in living organisms, without themselves being consumed in the reaction. Enzymes are highly specific for their substrates (usually catalysing only one particular reaction or a closely related set of reactions) and function efficiently under the mild conditions (temperature, pH) found within cells, typically by binding the substrate at a specific 'active site' on the enzyme.
steps: Enzymes = biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins
They catalyse specific biochemical reactions with high substrate specificity, working under mild physiological conditions via binding at a defined active site

question: What is the effect of denaturation on the structure of proteins?
solution: On denaturation, the secondary and tertiary structures of a protein (i.e. its specific, biologically active three-dimensional folded shape, held together by hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions) are disrupted and broken down, causing the protein to lose its native globular/fibrous conformation and unfold into a more random, extended structure. This unfolding is accompanied by loss of the protein's characteristic biological activity (e.g. a denatured enzyme loses its catalytic activity, as in the coagulation of egg white on boiling). Importantly, the primary structure (the covalent peptide bonds and sequence of amino acids) remains intact/unchanged during denaturation — only the higher-order (secondary, tertiary) folding is disrupted.
steps: Denaturation disrupts the weak, non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds etc.) responsible for the secondary/tertiary structure, causing the protein to unfold from its native conformation
This loss of specific 3D shape causes loss of biological activity (e.g. enzyme inactivation, egg white coagulation on boiling)
The primary structure (peptide bond sequence) itself remains unaffected by denaturation

question: How are vitamins classified? Name the vitamin responsible for the coagulation of blood.
solution: Vitamins are classified into two main groups based on their solubility: (1) Fat-soluble vitamins (soluble in fats/oils, and can be stored in the body's fatty tissue and liver) — includes vitamins A, D, E and K. (2) Water-soluble vitamins (soluble in water, generally not stored in the body in significant amounts and need regular dietary supply, with excess excreted in urine) — includes vitamin B-complex and vitamin C. Vitamin K is responsible for the coagulation (clotting) of blood.
steps: Vitamins are classified by solubility: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K — can be stored in the body) vs water-soluble (B-complex, C — generally not stored, need regular intake)
Vitamin K is specifically required for normal blood clotting/coagulation

question: Why are vitamin A and vitamin C essential to us? Give their important sources.
solution: Vitamin A is essential for maintaining good eyesight (it is required for the synthesis of the visual pigment rhodopsin in the retina); its deficiency causes a disease called xerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea) and night blindness. Important sources of vitamin A include fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is essential for maintaining the health of teeth, bones, gums and blood vessels, and for wound healing (it helps in collagen synthesis, and also boosts immunity); its deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, joint pain). Important sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits (amla/Indian gooseberry, oranges, lemons) and fresh green leafy vegetables.
steps: Vitamin A: needed for vision (rhodopsin synthesis), deficiency causes night blindness/xerophthalmia; sources include fish liver oil, carrots, butter, milk
Vitamin C: needed for healthy connective tissue/collagen, immunity, wound healing; deficiency causes scurvy; sources include citrus fruits, amla, green leafy vegetables

question: What are nucleic acids? Mention their two important functions.
solution: Nucleic acids are biopolymers of nucleotides (each nucleotide made of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group), found in the nucleus (and elsewhere) of living cells; the two types are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA). Two important functions: (1) They are responsible for the storage and transmission of hereditary (genetic) information from one generation to the next (DNA carries the genetic code). (2) They control and direct the synthesis of proteins in the cell (through the processes of transcription and translation, via messenger RNA, transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA).
steps: Nucleic acids = polymers of nucleotides (base+sugar+phosphate), comprising DNA and RNA
Function 1: carry/transmit hereditary (genetic) information across generations
Function 2: direct/control protein synthesis in cells

question: What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?
solution: A nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous (purine or pyrimidine) base attached to a pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) through a glycosidic bond, but WITHOUT any phosphate group. A nucleotide is formed when a phosphate group is additionally esterified onto the sugar of a nucleoside (typically at the 5' position), i.e. a nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate group, whereas a nucleoside = base + sugar only.
steps: Nucleoside = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar (no phosphate)
Nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate group (i.e. a phosphorylated nucleoside)

question: The two strands in DNA are not identical but are complementary. Explain.
solution: In the DNA double helix, the two polynucleotide strands are held together by specific hydrogen bonding between complementary nitrogenous bases on opposite strands, following strict base-pairing rules: adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T) via two hydrogen bonds, and guanine (G) always pairs with cytosine (C) via three hydrogen bonds. Because of this strict, specific pairing, wherever one strand has an A, the other strand must have a T at the corresponding position (and likewise G opposite C); consequently, the base sequence of one strand automatically determines (is complementary to, not identical to) the base sequence of the other strand — the two strands carry different (though corresponding/predictable) sequences of bases, which is why they are described as complementary rather than identical.
steps: DNA's two strands are held together by specific hydrogen-bonded base pairing: A pairs only with T (2 H-bonds), G pairs only with C (3 H-bonds)

This strict pairing rule means the sequence on one strand dictates (but does not duplicate) the sequence on the other strand — each base is matched with its specific different partner, not a copy of itself
Hence the two strands run with different (but predictably corresponding) sequences — they are complementary, not identical

question: Write the important structural and functional differences between DNA and RNA.
solution: Structural differences: (1) Sugar: DNA contains 2-deoxyribose sugar (lacking an –OH at C2'); RNA contains ribose sugar (has –OH at C2'). (2) Bases: DNA contains the pyrimidine base thymine (along with cytosine); RNA contains uracil instead of thymine (along with cytosine) — the purine bases adenine and guanine are common to both. (3) Strands: DNA is typically double-stranded (forming the famous double helix); RNA is typically single-stranded. Functional differences: DNA is the primary repository of genetic information, responsible for storing and transmitting hereditary information from generation to generation (self-replicating). RNA mainly functions in the expression of that genetic information — it is responsible for protein synthesis in the cell, existing in three main types: messenger RNA (mRNA, carries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome), transfer RNA (tRNA, brings specific amino acids to the ribosome), and ribosomal RNA (rRNA, forms part of the ribosome's structure).
steps: Structural: DNA has deoxyribose sugar + thymine + is double stranded; RNA has ribose sugar + uracil (instead of thymine) + is single stranded
Functional: DNA stores/transmits genetic (hereditary) information across generations; RNA (as mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) is primarily responsible for expressing that information via protein synthesis

question: What are the different types of RNA found in the cell?
solution: There are three main types of RNA found in cells, each with a distinct role in protein synthesis: (1) Messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries the genetic information (as a copy of the relevant DNA sequence) from the nucleus (DNA) to the ribosomes, where it serves as the template/code for protein synthesis. (2) Transfer RNA (tRNA), a smaller RNA that recognises specific codons on the mRNA and delivers the corresponding specific amino acid to the growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during translation. (3) Ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which, together with proteins, forms the structural and functional core of the ribosome, the cellular machinery on which protein synthesis actually takes place.
steps: Three types of RNA: mRNA (carries the genetic code from DNA to ribosome), tRNA (delivers specific amino acids matching mRNA codons during translation), and rRNA (structural/functional component of the ribosome itself)
